speechtext:

3.	No. The Civil Service Commission has on several occasions recommended to the Government the desirability of framing regulations which would remove from the Service married women whose husbands are able to support them; to require female employees to retire upon their marriage; and to prohibit the appointment of married women, save under certain exceptional and specified conditions. As a result an Order in Council was passed on the 18th June, 1920 (P.C. 1393), approving the following regulations:

Hereafter no married woman, whose husband is living, shall be eligible for appointment in the public service.
Provided that, when the commission reports that the supply of experienced help for any particular kind of work is not sufficient to meet the demands of the public service, a married woman may be certified for temporary employment.
Provided further, that where it can be established by a married woman that her husband is unable, through illness or other cause, to contribute to her support, such married woman may be certified for permanent or temporary employment.
Provided further, that where, in the opinion of the commission, it would be desirable or necessary, and in the best interests of the public service to employ a married woman or to employ husband and wife together, such married woman may be certified to by the commission for permanent or temporary employment.
A further Order in Council of the 12th March, 1921 (P.C. 517), provided that:
Any female employee in the public service shall, upon the occasion of her marriage, be required to resign her position.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext: I think the rule as to questions standing as Orders for Returns covers questions the answers to which would be lengthy, and consequently would be expensive to print. In regard to this question, the answer to the first question would be a certain figure, and the answer to the second question another figure.

I would draw the attention of my right hon. friend to the

second question asking how many civil servants in Canada are receiving $960 or less. This covers almost the entire civil service of the whole Dominion. If the question is allowed to stand on the Order Paper until we get that information it may be standing there for weeks. It is perfectly true, as my right hon. friend says, that the reply may not be very lengthy, but it will take a long time to obtain the desired information and in the meantime the question should not be allowed to remain on the Order Paper.

It is not to avoid the question standing on the Order Paper that the rule applies at all but only on account of the length of the answer. This is a very short question, and it would not matter if it stood1 all1 session.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It might be short, but the time required to obtain the information might be considerable. I think that is the real ground of the objection.

That is not the ground There is a rule, it was deliberated on this session, and I think a resolution passed by the committee. My recollection of it-and I am quite sure I am correct-is that it bears only on one point, the length of the answer, not the time to obtain it-the length of the answer and the consequent wisdom of putting it in Hansard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My recollection is that it is not a change of rule, but it had reference to the printing of long answers ir, Hansard. I think the proper procedure to be taken is that if the question can he answered quickly it should he answered, but if it requires the collection of information throughout the Dominion, it may require a very considerable time.
The rule says that it is for the Speaker to decide whether the question should he changed into an order for return.

I would say that the reasons given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) would indicate that this question should stand as an order for leturn, because I take it for granted that the question "How many civil servants in Canada are receiving salaries of $800 and less per annum" would require a great deal of work. It seems to me it covers a very wide range.

I suggest that the question should stand till your Honour could look up the rules to see whether

Questions
anything else is involved in this decision except the matter of the length of the answer.

I refer my hon. friend to rule 37, paragraph 4, which reads:
If a question is of such a nature that in the opinion of the minister who is to furnish the reply, such reply should be in the form of a return, and the minister states that he has no objection to laying such return upon the table of the House his statement shall unless otherwise ordered by the House be deemed an order of the House to that effect and the same shall be entered in the Votes and Proceedings as such.

Not at all. The minister may justify what he is doing now, but he cannot justify it in that way. The Civil Service Act went a certain length. It included virtually all the services; certain services did not come under it, for definite reasons given. Now, we went that distance and stopped there. But the minister is asking Parliament to retrace a part of the step that has been taken. He desires to remove something from the operation of the act by special statute, because he is afraid that otherwise the right man might not be appointed. To a certain length and stop is very different from what the minister proposes. Having got a certain distance, he wants us to retrace our steps and to that extent repeal the act.

speechtext: The Civil Service Act was passed before the Income Tax Act. speechtext:
My hon. friend is
entirely wrong. However, if we agree on the conclusion, I will not quarrel with him as regards the road we take to get there.

We may agree that
there is a great difference between never having brought certain services under the act, and seeking to make an exception of certain services that are already under it. The minister says that the exception here is justified on the ground that Mr. Russell has long experience and is, in his judgment, a man eminently qualified for the duties to which he is to be assigned. I am not disputing the minster's judgment. I know Mr. Russell, but I am not aware of his special qualifications. Assuming that the minister's judgment is correct, does he

Supply-Finance
think that the same fact would not appeal to the Civil Service Commission? Would Mr. Russell's long experience not appeal to them as eminently qualifying him?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They would have no right to consider it.
No right to consider his experience?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not in competition with another man.
Does the minister say that the Civil Service Commission cannot consider the experience of an applicant in estimating his qualifications?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not in competition with other applicants.

Certainly; in competition with others the applicant's experience in this case would help him in the race, just as it would help anybody else. The Civil Service Commission takes an applicant's experience into consideration, in fact, they do so in regard to every application. So that what the minister is doing is tantamount to saying that what really qualifies an applicant is something which the Civil Service Commission should not consider at all. If that is the case, then we should have no Civil Service Commission.
Hear, hear.
My hon. friends say " hear, hear." How many of them are there, though, who did not say just the opposite during the last three sessions?
Oh, no; we are quite consistent.

The Civil Service Act had all sorts of champions in this House, on this side of the Chamber, during the past three sessions. Even if we sought to refer to a committee the question whether or not it would be wise to make any exceptions, hon. gentlemen rose up in arms, indignant that anything should be done in the way of going back to patronage. But now they are enthusiastic advocates of such a course, because they think they will reap the rewards.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is entirely wrong in the basis of his argument. This is not a motion under which we are seeking to appoint a man. Mr. Russell was in the Civil Service. The superannuation order had been passed but had not taken effect. We did not need the Civil Service Commission to bring Mr. Russell into the service, because he was already a civil servant. All that we seek to do here, in the way of a departure from the act, is to give him a larger salary than he would have obtained under the Civil Service Act. He does not need the approval of the Civil Service Commission, because he was in the civil service. Superannuation had been ordered, but had not taken effect.

In his return the Civil Service Commission does not need to pass on his qualifications. It never did pass on them, as a matter of fact, because he was already in the service. That seems reasonable. But why should their jurisdiction in the matter of salary not apply?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Speaking generally, I suppose we have to accept a common principle. But I am going to submit that in the matter of salaries this House is a better judge than the Civil Service Commission; and on that ground, believing this to be a good appointment, I shall ask the House to give me authority to pay the increased salary. On that question I believe that this House is as good a judge as, if not better than, the Civil Service Commission, much as I respect their judgment.

I am sorry I cannot agree with the minister in that respect. If that judgment is correct, then the minister has no ground at all for remaining another hour under the jurisdiction of the commission. If we in this House are better judges of what a fair salary is for work done than is the Civil Service Commission, then the act has no just foundation, neither as respects the inside service nor the outside. I do not think the minister's reason is sound.

The minister has suggested a Commissioner of Taxation, and apparently the remarks of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) have reference to such an official. I notice, however, that the Supplementary Estimates refer to a Commissioner of Tariff.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If I said "Commissioner of Taxation," that is an error; " Commissioner of Tariff " is the proper term.

What are the duties of the Commissioner of Tariff?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To assist the minister in all inquiries into the tariff question. From beginning to end this matter is entrusted to the Finance Department. But the minister, with a fairly good impression of his own abilities, does not think he knows it all, and is anxious to procure assistance. He thinks that this gentleman is particularly capable and can help him in this service.
I was not in the House when the matter was first brought up, but my recollection is that Mr. Russell's former salary was $3,900.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that is correct.

My recollection, further, is that Mr. Russell, on the ground of advancing years and the necessity for rest, applied for superannuation, and on his insisting upon superannuation he was granted the sum of $2,700 a year. I should like to ask the minister whether the recalling of this superannuated gentleman-superannuated at his own request

will mean that the superannuation of $2,730 will be increased to what it would be on the basis of a salary of $6,000; or whether the appointment is looked upon by my hon. friend as of an entirely temporary nature, and that it is not intended to increase the superannuation allowance of $2,730.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The superannuation of an official is hardly under the control of a minister; it is fixed by law. My hon. friend says that this gentleman was retired at his own request. I hope that' is so. But he is still in very good health and has come back into the department at my particular request, for I regard him as a very valuable officer-a better one than I could get from among younger men I shall be glad if he stays in the department longer than he intended, but when the time comes for superannuation he will have to be retired under the terms of the Superannuation Act, that is, having regard to his average salary for the last three years. Undoubtedly if he continues in the department this will give him a larger superannuation than if he had remained out.
Approximately $4,300.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot say.
As against a superannuation of $2,730?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Quite so.
	.
It seems to me that under the exceptional circumstances this ought to be looked upon as a special appointment at the minister's request, without extending the gentleman's superannuation rates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would imply a change in the Superannuation Act, and for the present I do not contemplate such a change.

I do not pretend to have made any examination of the act, but I would think that on the recall of a superannuated officer his old superannuation would automatically apply upon his being released. If that is not the case, and if his being recalled for a temporary period has the effect of very substantially increasing his superannuation on account of an increased salary, I would think that a very serious objection to the proposal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Superannuation
Act will govern. If the operation of the act is such as my right hon. friend suggests, I have not any intention of changing it. I think he is mistaken. If that is the operation of the law, Mr. Russell will have to act accordingly.

We are at cross purposes. I think both my hon. friends are right. The cases put by the leader of the Opposition is the case of a man whose superannuation has taken effect and who is recalled. The case advanced by my hon. friend, the Minister of finance, is that of a man who is still in the service, and while superannuation has been applied for by him it has not yet taken effect; he is still being paid a salary. Under the circumstances I am afraid there is some chance of that happening which the minister says will happen-a very largely increased superannuation may be obtained.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If Mr. Russell remains in the service-and I hope he will-I hope he will get the benefit bf the average of his salary for the last three years, whatever it may be, and I do not think my hon. friend on reflection would wish it otherwise.

Knowing the great responsibilities that rest upon the Minister of Finance, do not hon. friends opposite feel that he is entitled to come to Parliament and ask for an appropriation for an officer in whom he has great confidence, and to expect to have such appropriation granted?
Supply-Finance

That applies to every minister. The point is that we do not know what obligation we are putting on the country by passing this vote. If it is a fact that by merely bringing Mr. Russell back for a temporary period it is going to have the effect of increasing his sup-annuation by $1,600 for all the rest of his life, that is one thing; if it is merely going to have the effect of giving him $6,000 for the temporary period, that is another thing. I would be under the impression that it would not have the more serious effect. But I think the committee should know what obligation will be incurred.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend is a legal gentleman and should be able to interpret the Superannuation Act better than I can be expected to. If Mr. Russell remains in the service two years longer -and I hope Re will-I 'think "he will be entitled to the full benefit of the Superannuation Act; if not, he will have to be content with my right hon. friend's interpretation.
The minister is a great deal older than I am, and his judgment ought to be better than mine in regard to this point.

You would
not think so.
I know the Prime Minister never had a very high opinion of my judgment.
The opinion seems to be reciprocal.

The Superannuation
Act contemplates a man coming into the service, continuing for a considerable length of time, and paying in a certain amount towards superannuation; then upon his retirement he would get superannuation based upon the average salary of the last three years. That would never contemplate a case like this. Mr. Russell came into the service forty years ago at a small salary, worked up until he reached $4,000, and then applied for and was entitled to superannuation on the basis of his salary the last three years, or $2,700. Now the minister proposes to fix a special salary by statute, and thereby entitle Mr. Russell to superannuation, based on that special salary for the rest of his life, even though he is only in the service for three years. Surely the minister does not suggest that
that was ever contemplated by the Superannuation Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The act will speak for itself.

This may mean thousands and thousands of dollars to Mr. Russell. Does the minister say that that was the original intention of the act? I am told it will mean $4,300 a year as against $2,700 a year, and Mr. Russell will get that all the rest of his life. If we are incurring that obligation we want to do it in the open; but the minister cannot say that that was ever the intention of the Superannuation Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The act says that superannuation applies on a man's retirement with due reference to his period of service, based on the average salary of the last three years. That is what the act says, that is our understanding in the case of Mr. Russell, and I cannot think the act contemplated anything else.

I happened to have some familiarity with this matter as it is now described by the minister. The firms he refers to were engaged in 1914 to perform certain legal services in the preparation of the trust mortgages connected with the Canadian Northern legislation and guarantee of that year. Bills were put in by these firms in the usual way-by the firm of Bain, Bickneil and Company, of Toronto, and by Lewis and Smellie, of Ottawa. These bills were taxed by the Justice Department in the usual way and the amount taxed was paid to each firm. Both firms, nevertheless, came back and insisted that they did not get enough and asserted that they would not submit to the taxation of the Justice Department. The government of that day, and every government since, insisted that the rule had to obtain and that the firms in question would have to abide by that taxation. If they could show anything that had not been .taxed; if they could show any services that had been rendered for which they did not submit a bill, all right; but we told them definitely that by the judgment of the taxing officer of the Justice Department the government was going to abide. That was the stand the late government took; the present Government takes a different stand and yields to their claims.

He was notified of his dismissal three days after he was dismissed; that was on the 1st of October, 1918, I understand.

He only knew he was going away three days after he was gone.
How long was Connor in the service, and what were the circumstances of his dismissal?

He was at Snow Flake, and his services were dispensed with on 1st October, 1918, but he did not receive notice until three days later, and he therefore made a claim for compensation. We have different reasons advanced from time to time why items are included in these supplementary estimates. My hon. friend, the Minister of Customs, has given us a particular reason in this case. He points out that there were delays in the reorganization of the department, that there was a proper vote from which these payments could be

Supply-Customs
made, but that they were not made because the accounts had not been checked and approved before the end of the last fiscal year. I understand that the purpose of these estimates is not to make good departmental faults, neglects or delays, but to provide for payments which have not been provided for in the main estimates of the year and have since become necessary. It seems to be quite obvious that this is not a vote of that character, and ought not to be included in these supplementary estimates. The Minister of Finance will appreciate that point.

I think that expenditure incurred last year, and not paid, ought not to be in the main estimates this year, but in the supplementary. In this case, instead of being short of funds, this item is due to the fact, as explained by the officers of the department, that the reorganization was not carried through in sufficient time for these accounts to be checked up and approved before the expiration of the fiscal year, 1920-21. Therefore it was necessary to have this amount voted before payment could be made. I think that is a proper item to come under the supplementary estimates.

It is pretty hard to say where the main estimates end and the supplementary estimates begin, and I suppose it is quite fair to give due appreciation to the position of my hon. friends. They seem to be cleaning up everything that has gone behind; they are making quite sure that everything that can be charged up will be charged up here.

Large numbers of destitute Canadian seamen in the United Kingdom have been repatriated to Canada by the British Board of Trade. The expenses thus incurred have been unusually large. There will be no necessity for further large expenditures of this kind, the abnormal conditions of shipping since the war, which have been responsible for there being so many destitute Canadian seamen in the United Kingdom, having now passed.

No, I understand this item covers the expenses incurred by the British Board of Trade 'over a period of three or four years.
Was an obligation entered into to pay this amount, and if so, when?

It has always been done, as my right hon. friend will understand. There is an agreement-at least, it is a custom-that the British Board of Trade takes charge of distressed Canadian seamen and the Canadian Government pays for the services thus rendered.

This further amount is required to meet the claim made by the Canadian Towing and Wrecking Company, Limited, of Port Arthur, Ontario, for services of the ice-breaker James Whalen during the spring of 1918. This company was instructed by the department to proceed with ice-breaking work in the spring of 1918 on a basis of cost. A claim for $50,000 was made and the department paid $18,750. The
5 p.m. company refused to accept this amount in full of account. It was claimed that no provision was made for cost repairs to the ice-breaker due to extremely heavy ice, and that the company suffered considerable financial loss, as owing to her being retained on this work a very favourable offer for the boat had to be refused. After discussion, the company offered to accept $16,000 in full of their claim for the balance of $31,250, without prejudice, and the Department of Marine is of the opinion that payment should be made on this basis, in view of the facts. I may add that this arrangement was made September or October last. I have no doubt that the settlement is good.
When was the settlement made for the payment of $16,000 in full?
In September or October last.

Since 1918. Part of the claim had been paid, but there was a further claim for $31,250. The company agreed to accept $16,000 in full, and the department agreed to pay that amount.
Would the minister tell us if this is to be in full settlement of all claims? I understood him to say it was accepted without prejudice.
Offered without prejudice.
Oh, offered without prejudice? Is it to be accepted in full settlement?
Yes. In full of their claim.

The company started furnishing in March, 1920, and the contract was cancelled by Order in Council on 18th February, 1921.

Well, I surmise they were taxed. All the Department of Marine and Fisheries had to do was to pay the amount as sent to it by the Department of Justice.

The case, I understand, is still pending. An amount of $3,000,000 has been paid to the Dominion Iron and Steel Company in virtue of an agreement. I am not supposed to speak for the Department of Justice, but my hon. friend will understand that the lawyers who are employed there attend to the internal work of the department- they do not usually plead before the courts on behalf of the department.

It is still unsettled.
And this $3,000,000 was paid before the litigation was decided?

As I explained to my hon. friend, an agreement was entered into between the government and the company by which the company accepted, I think, $4,600,000 as a settlement. The government had to give its final answer accepting that agreement one month after the first $3,000,000 was paid-they were paid on account at the price set out in the agreement. If after one month the balance was not paid the agreement was cancelled altogether, and that is what has happened. The case is still before the courts.
It seems to me a rather strange procedure for the late government to pay $3,000,000 to any company in Canada for damages while the suit was still in course of settlement?

Referring to the remarks of the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Lanctot) as to the engagement of outside counsel I quite agree with the minister that it is necessary to go outside very often for counsel; but I would recommend to the hon. member that he continue his pressure regularly, insistently,

and increasingly because it will probably be needed.
I will.

As to the remarks of the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff), if he will refer back some years- many years in fact, particularly between 1896 and 1911-he will find many cases of settlement in that period. This, however, was not a case of settlement. The company offered to settle at a certain amount which counsel for the government and the officers of the Justice Department recommended. I think the amount was what the minister says, $4,600,000, and their claim was in the neighbourhood of $10,000,000,- I cannot recall the exact amount. There was no question in the judgment of ourselves, or in the judgment of anyone engaged in the case, that the company had suffered very considerably but it was essential, it could not be helped. They were out of the money and as a consequence there was a very considerable lack of proceeding in their work, and although we were recommended, and strongly recommended, by our own officers to settle for $4,600,000 we took this step: We paid the $3,000,000 to enable them to go on witn their work without which they would not have been able to go on, and we left it to the incoming government to decide whether they would accept the settlement by paying the balance, or whether they would go on with the litigation. As to which course they should pursue I have nothing to say. They have decided to go on with the litigation and the court will decide whether there is any balance and, if so, what it is. I submit the proceeding was right, particularly in the interest of the territory affected and in the interest of all concerned.

The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) desires me to run backwards to 1896. This is the year of our Lord, 1922. I do not intend to run forward and backward. We should settle this matter on its merits this year. If the Dominion Iron and Steel Company had a claim against this Government, no money should have been paid until that claim was settled by litigation, or compromise, or some other way. If the Government owed the Dominion Iron and Steel Company this money, they should have had the courage of their convictions, and should have paid, not $3,000,000, but $4,600,000. That would have been the business way. But, as in everything else they did, they compromised the matter, and paid the Dominion Iron and
Steel on November 25, 1921, just three weeks before the election, the sum of $3,000,000; and then, knowing that they were not going to be elected, left the balance to be settled by the new government.

I want to come back to the lawyers. The Department of Justice has about ten lawyers at least, and my right hon. friend, the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen), told the House that sometimes we have to go outside for lawyers. I am a farmer as hon. members know, and if I have ten employees, and have some work to do outside my farm, I take a few of my employees outside to do the work. I understand in this case the hearing was in Ottawa and the court sat in Ottawa. Why could they not take a couple of lawyers from the Department of Justice to defend the action? Why go outside and pay $70,000 for counsel? Someone refers to the fact that it was just before the election, and that the $3,000,000 was paid during the election campaign. Why not wait until after the election? That is the part of it that I do not understand. When my hon. friend advises me to watch this Government, my answer is that I will do so.

I would presume, from what I have read in regard to the Grand Trunk Arbitration case, that a great part of this item would be engineers' fees, disbursements for engineers, actuaries and so on, and I would recommend to the hon. member that, if it is money he is seeking in life, he should take one of those professions.
I am not seeking for money at all.
If he intends to get into the government employ-

I do not care for money.
Mr.- MEIGHEN: It is the late government who are responsible for whatever selections were made of counsel in that action. But when you have a subsidy of $250 apiece for the 4,000 people in the country, it seems to me the matter might well be inquired into.

What is this large amount? In the general estimates we have a very large amount for Dominion parks, and this is a very large amount in the Supplementary Estimates. I notice that this amount was spent last year by Governor General's warrant. What is the reason?

An amount of $115,000 was provided in the Estimates for the fiscal years 1921-22 in connection with work on the Banff-Windermere highway in Kootenay park, British Columbia. About the middle of August this amount was ex-
Supply-Interior

hausted and as the minister considered it desirable to carry on operations until late in the fall rather than close down the work and force approximately 140 men out of employment, an Order in Council was passed on the 13th August, 1921, P.C. 2917, recommending that a Governor General's warrant should issue for the sum of $50,000. With this extra amount, an additional twelve miles of road was constructed and nine miles of clearing of the right of way was completed.
By an agreement with the British Columbia government executed in 1919, the Dominion government agreed to complete this road by January, 1924, and to ensure the fufilment of this agreement, it was considered advisable in the month of October to continue operations as long as winter conditions would permit, and an Order in Council was passed on the 17th October, 1921, P.C. 3892, recommending that a Governor General's warrant should issue for a further sum of $16,500. With the additional work done, there is every possibility that the roads will be completed in 1922, and that Canada will begin to derive benefits from the increased tourist revenue in the season of 1922-23, as this is the only uncompleted section of what is probably the most spectacular automobile route in the world, namely: an international circuit highway connecting the Pacific coast, the Grand Canyon of Colorado, Yellowstone and Glacier parks of the United States and all the various cities of the southwestern states with Banff and the Canadian National parks. It is estimated that the first year that this highway is open will increase Canada's tourist revenue by some three million dollars.
In view of the unemployment which existed in the West during the late fall and the possibility of its continuing throughout the winter months, the question of providing employment on necessary construction works in the different parks was carefully considered, and as the working organizations in the various parks, and as the field engineering forces were such that the different works could be economically carried on, an Order in Council was passed on the 12th November, 1921, P.C. No. 4319, recommending that a Governor General's warrant should issue for the sum of $100,000. This provided work for approximately 215 men for a period of four months during a time when such employment was necessary to relieve possible distress.
To keep the men busy during the last campaign.

The suspicious member will note that the decision was arrived at long before there was any decision for a campaign. He is a little off the mark. This is something for which we take full responsibility, and the explanation given by the Prime Minister is precisely the explanation that actuated the late government in its decision. We intended to perform a certain amount of work last year and we provided the money for the purpose. Owing to two considerations, the primary one being the need of providing employment in that district and particularly from Calgary where the need was very great-and I am sure, had the hon. member (Mr. Lanetot) seen the petitions that we received and learned the facts that we learned, he would have done everything he could to have relieved the conditions-we decided to go on further. It was a work that had to be done and one that would provide a revenue as soon as, or sooner than, any other work that we could have performed. It was work in which practically all of the money was going to the labouring man; it was work on this highway that had been going on during the summer. As the Prime Minister says, the anticipated revenue to the people of Canada from that road when completed is expected in the first year to be $3,000,000. It surely was the part of wisdom to utilize the occasion and give the work when it was most needed, in view of the fact that the revenue would come so soon. I hope, in the course we took, we shall have the support of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) because, if there is anything he should be interested in, it is this. This is a case where unemployment was relieved, and not where it was promised and left unrelieved.

I notice by the main estimates that in 1921-22 the sum of $800,000 was voted for Canadian National parks. For the same purpose we are asked to vote, if I remember the Prime Minister's statement rightly, $150,000 for extra moneys spent by the late government. The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) gives, as the reason for an expenditure of almost a million dollars, the fact that it gave employment.

Oh, no. My hon. friend has mistaken the figures. I forget what the Prime Minister gave as the amount of the appropriation, but the hon. member is astray.

speechtext: That is prophetic.
If the leader of the Opposition will turn to page 57 of the Main Estimates he will see that in 1921-22 $800,000 was voted. We shall see whose arithmetic is wrong.
All right.
Part of that $800,000 was for salaries and part for administration, and the $115,000 I have already mentioned was for the roads themselves.

The amount spent on this road for everything is $115,000. The hon. member is referring to the Banff-Windermere road, and the amount in last year's estimates for this work was as the Prime Minister has stated. This is an extra amount spent; the balance has nothing to do with that road at all.

I am referring to the
amount spent on Canadian National parks, and I presume that this $115,000 is part of the total of $915,000 spent on that work last year. While, of course, it is a very good thing to try to make good roads all over the country and in this way incidentally relieve unemployment, of which we had
so much last year, I do not see any more reason why we should spend this money on the Canadian National parks than anywhere else. The leader of the Opposition says that in three or four years' time we shall have a revenue of a few million dollars from the roads in this particular part of the country. Well, the same thing might be said in regard to the roads in any other part of Canada. If the Government spent a million dollars in Nova Scotia we should have thousands of tourists there who would spend a large amount of money. The same thing might be said of New Brunswick or of Quebec, particularly the latter province, into which there would be a large influx of tourists. But that, I contend, is no good reason why $915,000 should be spent in one particular part of the country; nor is it a good reason, even, that the expenditure of this money would relieve unemployment. Other provinces in the Dominion have had a good deal of unemployment, but they did not come to the Government with a request that money should be spent on the roads to relieve that unemployment. The provincial governments took charge of that problem, and to a certain extent the citizens themselves have endeavoured to find a way out of the difficulty. Those who could not find employment in their own particular vocations sought work in other lines. I see no good reason why, on the eve of an election, this large amount of money should have been voted by the late government and spent in this way. The late government, in my opinion, deserves in this respect the censure not only of this House but of the country at large.

I entirely disagree with the remarks of the member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff). I think the late government are to be complimented on having pushed this work on during the last fall and winter, having practically completed it with the exception of a few miles. And I desire to compliment the present Government, as well, upon their foresight in realizing the necessity of completing this particular work at the earliest possible date, because I have every confidence that what the Prime Minister says is absolutely correct, that the finishing of this road, completing as it does, what is known as the Grand Circle Tour, will mean millions of money to this country and will repay very amply indeed the investment which this Government makes. Now, it is quite true that you might expend money in Nova

Scotia with the result of bringing a number of tourists to that part of our country. But I think there are few who will question the fact that the expenditure of this sum of money-spent, mind you, by virtue of an agreement with the province of British Columbia-is certainly a far better investment, from the tourist point of view, than any expenditure of a similar amount that might be made in Nova Scotia. I compliment the past government on their energy in carrying on this work; and the present Government, in providing for it this year, is doing a great service indeed, not only in meeting the difficult unemployment conditions that exist in that part of Canada, but also in completing the work in order that returns may be secured from the investment at the earliest possible date.

While the estimates in connection with the Parks branch of the Interior Department were under consideration I did not happen to be in my seat, and if I am in order at the present time I should like, with the permission of the committee, to revert to the former item in order to discuss a question with reference to migratory birds. This question comes under the Parks branch, I believe, and with the consent of the committee I would Tike to'refer to certain resolutions that have been forwarded to me, and no doubt to other hon. gentlemen from the maritime provinces who are interested in this matter.
I think the hon. member would be quite in order in dealing with the matter under this item. The question of migratory birds comes under National parks.

When the
Migratory Birds Act was put into operation it seems to have worked 'beneficially to all the provinces except Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick. In the two latter provinces it has created a great deal of dissatisfaction. The close season starts, I think, on the first of March, and that is about the time the birds migrate northward. This is the onlv time of the year that the people in the province of Prince Edward Island have an opportunity to get any birds in their migration north. Fishermen and sportsmen are allowed to shoot the birds only on their return in the fall, and it is practically impossible for them to get any birds at that time of the year. The matter has been taken up by the legislatures of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, and

resolutions passed by these two bodies have been forwarded to me. I do not wish to take up the time of the committee reading them, but the resolution from Prince Edward Island, after setting forth the various reasons for the opinion it expresses, concludes as follows:
Be it therefore resolved that in the opinion of this assembly the shooting of geese and brant in this province is only practicable in the stpring and then only for a very short period and that the prohibition in this province of the spring shooting of these birds is not only wholly unnecessary for their protection but on the other hand operates as a discrimination against this province in that it amounts to practically a total prohibition of the shooting of these birds at any time, and this assembly is strongly of the opinion that this province should be excepted from the operations of the said act in so far as the season of shooting of geese and brant is concerned but that the present provincial game laws or similar regulations regarding the shooting of migratory birds should be adequately enforced and that this would afford ample protection to the birds and would sufficiently conform to the spirit of the said federal act and the treaty upon which it is based.
And that the act 7-8 George V, chapter 18, should be so amended as to permit the spring shooting of brant and geese in this province.
A similar resolution was passed by the government of Nova Scotia at the instance of Mr. Kinley, member for Lunenburg. It is as follows:
Whereas the federal Government, by virtue of the Migratory Bird Treaty, has acquired and assumed jurisdiction over migratory birds in the province of Nova Scotia.
Therefore resolved that the provisions of the Fish and Game Act relating to the protection of such birds should be repealed.
A committee of the House be appointed to review the regulation made by the Dominion Government under said treaty, for the purpose of recommending such changes as the conditions in Nova Scotia may require.
Possibly it is beyond the power of this House to deal with the matter, as an international treaty is involved, but I wish to point out that this treaty works an injustice to the people of that province. A few days ago some five or six men who happened to be out with their fire arms were arrested, although they had not shot a bird, and were taken before a magistrate twenty-five miles away, who fined them $25 each. This was rather harsh treatment. We are not in favour of slaughtering these birds for market purposes; but fishermen and sportsmen claim that they should have the privilege of shooting a few in the only season of the year that they can get near them during their migratory flight to the north. Only a few days ago I noticed an item in the newspapers describing the destruction of fishermen's nets by brant,

Supp ly-In te rior
gulls and other birds. In order to get at the fish in the nets these birds tear the nets to such an extent ,that they become almost useless, yet the fishermen are not allowed to fire a shot to scare the birds away. These men are only asking that they be allowed to take a few birds in their flight north, which is the only time that they have any chance of bagging them.

We complain of the
Americans shooting migratory birds in the spring just before they come north to breed. How can we justify the shooting of these same birds after they have left the South?
Do they not shoot those birds up to the first of March?
No, they do not; the spring shooting is done away with under the new agreement.
When was that amendment made?
Last year. If you will look up our own game laws, you will find that to be the case.
The complaint our people had was that the Americans could shoot those birds from March first, whereas on the 2nd of March in our country we were not allowed to take a single bird.
That was true up to last year.

That was
where it was so unfair.
It was unfair.

Is there not a season in the fall when our people can shoot these migratory birds? I have heard no complaint in my part of the country against the close season in the spring of the year. It does seem to me that my hon. friend is complaining because two of his friends have been "pinched".

No, they did not happen to be my friends. They were from another county. There is no complaint from my friends; they obey the law. In the fall of the year they claim it is impossible to shoot any of those birds on their return south because they stay far out to sea, very few of them frequenting the estuaries of our rivers. Their feeding place is out at sea where they are beyond the reach of our sportsmen.

I desire to support my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. MacLean). I have heard many complaints in my own county against this law. As far back as a hundred years ago I understand there was no closed season for migratory birds, and to-day they are just as numerous as they were at that time, so I do not think there is any fear of their extermination by allowing our people to shoot a few in the spring season.

The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) said that perhaps the reason why the member for Prinrfe (Mr. MacLean) brought this subject to the attention of the committee was that some of his friends bad been fined for violating the provisions of the Migratory Birds Act I am glad to know that this Government deals differently with offenders against the la'w to what the 'late government did. I had a case in my county last fall where two young men, contrary to the provisions of the act, shot some df those birds. They were haled before a magistrate, the Department of Justice retained a solicitor to prosecute them, and were found guilty and each fined $30 and costs. Some good friend of the late government telegraphed to Ottawa, with the result that the present leader of the Opposition passed one of his famous Orders in Council, remitting to these young men the fines which the magistrate had imposed. This happened three or four days before the general election last December. That is the way the late government carried out the provisions of the Migratory Birds Act.

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
I desire to add a word or two to the observations made by the hon. member for Prince, P.E.I. The people of Nova Scotia object that while they are prohibited from shooting these birds in the spring, when they return from the northern latitudes in the fall, nice and plump and fat, the American sportsmen get at them. It is quite impossible for our sportsmen to shoot these birds after the spring, as they remain for a short time only along the coast of the maritime provinces, and then proceed to the north and stay there until fall. On their return, as the hon. member for Prince has said, they do not land m the estuaries of our rivers, but feed out at sea and then proceed south. That is the time that the American sportsmen, having no close season, can shoot them as they return plump and palatable after feeding upon the fertile pastures of the northern latitudes. This Migratory Birds'
Ifigg	COMMONS

Treaty is an entirely one-sided, jug-handled agreement. It is unfair to the people of the maritime provinces. I am not speaking for the so-called "sportsmen." I have no sympathy with men who go out and shoot these birds purely for "sport"; but I have sympathy for the men living along the coast of the maritime provinces who shoot these birds only because they regard them as a prime necessity. While under the terms of the present Migratory Birds Act they are deprived of that privilege at the only season of the year when It can be of any use to them, sportsmen across the boundary have the full benefit and advantage of shooting these birds without any limitation whatever.

I hope that the remarks which have been addressed to the committee by some hon. members against the provisions of the Migratory Birds Treaty Act and the convention between Canada and the United States in that regard will not have the effect of lessening in any way the restrictions applied under that act and agreement. You may find in isolated districts complaints coming from, I may say, selfish people who want to continue to kill these migratory birds in the spring of the year when they should be protected from sportsmen and people who pretend they depend on their flesh for food. Who ever heard of people living in Canada who depended on the flesh of wild geese in the spring for their food? These birds that have been spoken of-the brant and the duck-are scarcely fit to eat; they are thin and emaciated. My hon. friend spoke of the brant breaking up the fishermen's nets in an effort to get fish; apparently he does not know that the brant is not a fish-eating bird-not a diver, even. When the provisions of the convention between the United States and Canada were first put into force in Canada, there was an inclination-and I may say that I was somewhat affected that way myself-to complain against these restrictions which prevented the very fine spring shooting we used to get. In the case of the Yukon Territory these restrictions involve more hardship, perhaps, than in any other part of Canada; the fall comes so early there that the main flight of the birds is gone even before the open season commences, and in the spring there is as good shooting as can he had any where in the world. The birds come there in millions, on their way to the breeding grounds a short distance further north; you could shoot any

amount of them. I am bound to admit that since the Migratory Birds Convention Act was put into force the fall shooting has been very much improved, and I think that applies all over Canada. If these provisions are observed by the people of the United States and Canada, the number of birds which can be hunted in the fall in both countries will very soon be materially increased.

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip
speechtext: The hon. member for Yukon expresses surprise that there are any people in Canada who would really use these birds for food. I say they are very much more palatable than the dog-meat that is sometimes, of necessity, eaten by the people in other parts of Canada. Circumstances may arise which make it necessary for people to go out and shoot these birds for food, just as circumstances may arise in the northern country under which people go out and obtain dog-meat for food.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That discussion can take place on the Main Estimates.
But this item has relation to the policy of the Government with respect to the Welland Ship Canal.

When we
take up the Main Estimates a discussion can take place on the whole canal question.

This involves a matter of policy and the item is a very large one. I wish to offer some observations in respect to it, but I promise not to be very long. In my opinion this project has not been handled in the way it should have been handled. We had a statement from the minister the other day that the Welland ship canal will not be ready to be opened until 1-927. Now this canal is a most important link in the whole route for water borne traffic from the city of Montreal to the head of the lakes. Until it is completed the larger boats on the upper lakes will be unable to come down to lakes Erie and Ontario. At present a barge carrying
500,000	bushels of grain, when it reaches Fort Colborne, has to have its cargo transshipped to two or three smaller barges and conveyed to the city of Montreal at an additional cost of four or five cents per bushel. This transhipment diverts a large part of the grain intended for Montreal into other channels. According to a report brought down at an earlier date by the International Joint Commission, a great part of this grain now goes to Buffalo. I do not say that the minister is responsible for this state of but it is exceedingly unfortunate. The Erie canal which was started about the same time as the Welland canal, or shortly afterwards, has been completed and is now open, with the result that the former is getting a large bulk of the business which should pass through Canadian channels. If the same vigour had been displayed m prosecuting this particular work that was shown in the deepening of the Queens-ton and Chippawa canal, the Welland should be ready to be opened in about two years. Until this work is finished we shall not derive the value that we ought to receive from the large expenditure which the people of Canada have made upon this canal system. Consequently the ports on lake Huron and the 'Georgian, bay, and on lake Erie and lake Ontario, as well as those on the St. Lawrence route are going to suffer. Now, according to information disclosed to the House, $30,000,000 have been spent on this project already and no-

body knows when it is going to be finished; it is an eye-sore in the Niagara district to-day. If the work on the Welland canal was vigorously prosecuted it could be completed in a year or two and the large boats on the upper lakes would be able to reach lake Erie and lake Ontario. The result would be that we should have some regulation of the rates for five or six months in the year as between the railways and the water routes. The importance of getting this canal finished is fully set out in the report of the International Joint Commission. I know the minister has given consideration to the important factor which the immediate completion of the Welland canal will prove in lessening the rates on wheat from the great West. I do not wish to detain the House to-night with any further remarks. I hope, however, that when we take up the Main Estimates the Government will disclose the fact that they are so seized with the importance of the subject that they will give effect to the recommendations of the International Joint Commission who Investigated this problem. We are away behind the times in our handling of this great project. The Erie canal will have been in operation, I think, this year, for the third summer, and the people of the United States are deriving great benefit from the use of this channel of communication. And it was a most important factor, as Mr. Hoover said the other day. Of course Mr. Hoover is a very high authority and is doing good work in lowering the high cost of living in the United States. He said that when the Welland canal was finished we would get the results in cut rates that this great canal would force. While I have every confidence in the minister, I hope when the Main Estimates are brought down he will give the House and the committee some idea as to when the canal is going to be finished.

I understand that in the Main Estimates last year $5,000,000 was appropriated for the work of this canal, and I want to know who authorized further expenditure of nearly half a million dollars for the extension of this work. We understand that when $5,000,000 is voted the people who are responsible for continuing this work will keep within that amount; otherwise we will have no say in the matter as to how far it shall be exceeded until the work is done, and we are asked to vote a supplementary estimate. I do not wish to go into the matter of the Welland canal at this particular period, but it seems to

me that that canal will become a competing factor with the two transcontinental railways. At the present time the railways do not pay, and before the Welland canal can be completed and put on a paying basis, it would be of great interest to this country to continue the branch line service to the farmers, in order that they might be able to get their products to the trunk lines and transcontinental lines and give the men some work to do. For that reason, instead of continuing to expend $5,000,000 and a supplementary estimate of nearly $500,000,1 think it would be to the interest of the country at large, and would also put the two transcontinentals on a paying basis, if this money, providing there is any to be spared, should be spent in extending the branch lines to the real sources of the products that will be carried over them.
