The Grand Trunk Railway placed orders for 29,000 tons.
Dominion Iron & Steel, 15,243 at $49 ton f.o.b. mill.
Algoma, 13,828 at $49 ton f.o.b. mill.
Orders were for delivery in April and May, payment to be made in May and June. No payments have yet been made. The balance, 6,000 tons, was not ordered.

At what price were
these orders placed? What was the cost of the service?

Dominion
Iron and Steel Company $49 per ton f.o.b. the mills. That was for firsts, and for seconds $46.55 per ton f.o.b. the mill. The Algoma price was $50 per ton f.o.b. the mill for firsts, and $47.50 f.o.b. the mill for seconds. Of the orders placed by the Grand Trunk Railway, the one with the Dominion Iron and Steel company of 15,243 tons was placed at $49 per ton f.o.b. the mill, and the one with the Algoma Steel Company of 13,828 tons, at $49 a ton f.o.b. the mill.
What are the current prices for rails?
We have not been on the market for rails since then, and I am not in a position to give the hon. member the information.

Are these rails being
utilised, or are they still on hand?

They are
being distributed and used for replacement purposes.
I understood the minister to say in his speech, that there were to he no extensions of lines this year. It would be a good plan to use the rails on branch lines.

They are
being used for replacement purposes.



Supply-Railways and Canals

In connection with this item, I should like to explain to the committee that, in the closing months of 1921, very strong representations were made, not only to the Department of Railways and Canals and the government, but to the boards in charge of the operation of Canadian-owned railways, that the unemployment situation in large centres of industrial activity throughout Canada was such that a very great hardship was likely to result to the working people during the winter season of 1921-22. It was urged, not only upon the boards of management of the two systems, but upon the government, and urged by representatives of municipalities, by boards of trade, by labour organizations, by, in fact, all interests, that the railways should, as far as possible, anticipate their requirements; that orders likely to be, placed for the season of 1922, should be so placed that the industries could be operated during the winter season. That is exactly what was done. The government conferred with the Canadian Northern board and the Grand Trunk board and suggested to them that it would be well that, having regard to the unemployment situation, they should take into consideration the advisability of placing these orders. It was decided that the two boards, having determined what the possible requirements for this season would be in the way of rails and having taken stock of the cars that were in hand and would be required to be replaced or repaired for the season's operations, should place orders for repair and reconstruction of cars and orders for rails for replacement purposes, and the action of the government was confined to providing in anticipation the funds. It was in pursuance of this policy that the government, in carrying out the Order in Council referred to by the minister, authorised the boards and undertook to provide the funds.

I am a little surprised to hear the ex-minister (Mr. Stewart) say that those contracts were given out just to relieve unemployment in some parts of the country. Does he not know that all this work of repairing cars could have been given to the shops of the railways in the province of Quebec or elsewhere? From the very fact that the exminister gave that work out to some private corporations he reduced the number of men in the railway shops. They were turned out and added to the ranks of the unemployed in

other parts of the country just for the sake of those private corporations of which the government that was in power at that time was so fond. I was greatly distressed to see hundreds of men turned out in the cold of winter just because private corporations wanted to have those contracts notwithstanding the hardship inflicted upon the men who were working in the shops at Riviere du Loup. I am surprised at my hon. friend coming boldly before such a House as this and supporting the firing out of these men into the cold just for the sake of some private corporations.

In reply to the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Gauvreau), I should like to explain to the committee that neither the late government nor the Department of Railways and Canals had any part to play in placing the orders. I am sure the boards in control of the shops to which my hon. friend refers, would place those orders, having due regard to the requirements of their staffs. The orders for rails were distributed amongst the companies which were engaged in the manufacture of rails. Some of the orders went to the Algoma Steel Company and the balance to Nova Scotia. In the repair and reconstruction of cars as also, for that matter, in connection with placing orders for rails, regard was had to the question of unemployment, and the Order in Council which authorized the orders which were placed, provided that, in the placing of those orders, conference should be had with the Department of Labour in order that the work should go to relieve unemployment, and not as my hon. friend (Mr. Gauvreau) states, to private corporations for any considerations outside of that of unemployment, because no order could be placed until after conference with the Minister of Labour and until after the situation in the locality where an order was placed had been canvassed and surveyed, regard being had to the question of employment at the time and also to the question of possible employment during the winter season.
Do I understand that the Minister of Labour decided where those orders would be placed?

I hope the committee did not understand me as apparently the hon. member for Marquette did. I said that the orders were anticipated in order, as far as was consistent with good business and management, to relieve the unemployment situation. The

Supply-Railivays and Canals
government having that in view, it was decided that, in the placing of orders, the boards should appreciate exactly what the unemployment situation was, and the records in the Department of Labour gave that information to an extent that it would have been impossible to get it in any other way. The hon. gentleman hardly states the situation as it existed. Unemployment was at the basis of the whole policy, and the late government was very careful to impress upon the two boards that, in anticipating the requirements upon which those orders would be based, due regard should be had to what was to be required this year. And it was provided that while these companies were to go on and manufacture, payment was not to be made until delivery. They could go on and make rails and pile them up, but payment by the board was to be made at the time that delivery was taken; and delivery would be taken when the requirement arose.

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
While this item is under
consideration I would draw to the attention of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Kennedy) the conditions of unemployment that exist in the city of Sydney at the present time, and have existed for some months past. The city of Sydney has been built up around the steel industry which was established there many years ago. It is one of our best markets-in fact it is the best market that we have locally-for the consumption of the coal which is produced in the island of Cape Breton. As the member for Lanark (Mr. Stewart) stated, an order was given last year in anticipation of the requirements of the government railways, and that order had a very considerable effect in relieving the unemployment situation as it existed in that centre of population some months ago. Unfortunately, however, owing to the depression that prevails throughout all the avenues of trade in the maritime provinces and in Canada generally, no general orders for the manufacture of steel have been secured by steel companies.
The plant in Sydney a year ago employed some 4,000 persons who, with their families, constitute the largest proportion of the population of the city. But the number of employees was reduced some months ago to 800. There are to-day, and have been for some months, 3.200 steel workers in idleness in that city. The city has been unable to collect taxes from these people for the simple reason that they have no money wherewith to pay them; and as a conse-
107i
quenee the civic officers have not been paid their salaries for more than a month. That is a condition that ought not to exist in any part of this country if it can possibly be obviated.
The late government did very well in placing the orders which they gave in anticipation of the requirements of the government railways but I do think that the present Minister of Railways, in further anticipation of the needs of the Government railways in the matter of rails, should give an order to the steel company at Sydney for, say, 25,000 tons, so that the steel plant there might start again and provide much needed employment to the steel workers of that community.
Now, Sydney is unfortunately situated with respect to the receiving of orders from other railway corporations in Canada. Up to the present time the steel company at Sydney has never received an order for steel rails from the Canadian Pacific Railway, for the reason that the Canadian Pacific railway line does not extend to the city of Sydney, and that company are averse to paying freight on the rails to another railway corporation. Therefore, so far as the purchase of rails in Canada goes, the Canadian Pacific Railway places its orders with the rival plant at Sault Ste. Marie in the province of Ontario. The same has been true with respect to rails purchased by the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk Railway Company. They have placed their orders for steel rails entirely with the steel plant in Ontario.
The Dominion Government has owned a railway in the maritime provinces for many years. That railway is now linked up with the Canadian National Railway System, and I submit that in the very near future there must be a necessity for very large orders of rails for this government system. Even though the Minister of Railways may have on hand a sufficient quantity of rails for the present year, I do not think that, taking into consideration the conditions as they exist in Sydney to-day, and having regard to the desire of all classes in Canada to relieve as far as possible the unemployment situation throughout the country, the Government would be justified in placing another order with the steel company at Sydney for the purpose of relieving unemployment. I am told by gentlemen who are experts in' the matter of the value of steel rails, that steel rails are the one commodity which do not deteriorate while not in use. On the contrary, they increase in value and use-

Supply-Railways and. Canals
fulness with age, and I am informed that the Government would not be losing anything even if they were to pay interest on money borrowed for the purpose of placing another order with the steel company at Sydney, because the value of the rails, as regards durability, would have increased so much by being kept in storage for a year or two, that the additional cost would be more than compensated for.
I trust that the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), who after all is the one member of the Government that has to provide the wherewithal to meet the demands that would be made in connection with these additional orders, will be able to find the means whereby an order can be placed in Sydney. I do not think it would be fair to place the cost of these rails against the operating account of the railways for the present year, because the rails would not be used until probably 1923. I think it would be worth while for the Government to consider the proposal to borrow a certain sum of money to defray the cost of the rails; but the cost should not appear in the accounts for the operation of the Railway Department for 1922 or 1923. Now, this is a most serious matter, and besides bringing it up before this committee to-night, my colleague (Mr. Carroll) who is at present engaged on a committee in another part of the building and myself have taken it up with the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Finance, and I give notice now that at a very early date we hope to renew the application for this order. I trust therefore that the Government may find some way, in view of the conditions that prevail to-day, to accede to the request and get the steel rail mills going once more in the city of Sydney.

I occasionally find myself in agreement with the sentiments expressed by the genial Whip on the Government side (Mr. Kyte). But I must, in the strongest manner possible, dissent from the strange and remarkable doctrine which he has just propounded to the House. I sympathize very deeply indeed with the position of the steel workers in the town of Sydney; but I take this opportunity, Mr. Chairman, to draw the attention of this House to the fact that the condition that exists in Sydney to-day is indeed a striking commentary on the whole public policy that has been followed in the past in respect of the steel industry in Canada. The official records will disclose the fact that in the past this 
Dominion has subsidized the steel industry of Canada to the tune of between $15,000,000 and $20,000,000. I cannot speak with exact knowledge of the precise amount; but I know it is somewhere between the figures I have mentioned. Now, what have we got? We have given out in cold cash to the steel companies in this Dominion somewhere between $15,000,000 and $20,000,000 in the way of actual bonus to build up their business for the purpose of creating these industries in Canada and giving employment to Canadian labour. And after having done all that, we are faced now with the remarkable doctrine that we must further subsidize this particular industry by placing government orders with it in order that the workmen who have been gathered around it may be enabled to live. If that is a wise, sane and sound method of developing the country, then I certainly have a great deal to learn. I will make that confession very fully and very frankly.
The Minister of Railways will be ill-advised indeed as far as the Government is concerned if he is governed by any other than the soundest business principles in the placing of orders for the National Railways. One of the criticisms I have to make against the late government in respect to these particular orders that we are now discussing, is, that in my judgment they were not placed according to sound business principles. I am not going to draw further attention to the significant fact that they were placed a few months prior to the election. My hon. friend, the late Minister of Railways (Mr. Stewart) states that this was done to relieve unemployment.
And good Liberals were dismissed from the shops.

I accept his assurance in that respect, but the significance of the time at which the orders were placed is not lost. We find that orders for rails were placed at $50 a ton. I am not aware at what price rails could be purchased today, but I think I am well within the mark when I say that they could be purchased at very considerably less than that figure. That illustrates one of the business practices that should be followed in the operation of the Canadian National Railways,- that rails, cars, and all other equipment and rolling stock required for their operation should be purchased at the lowest prices. It is not a sound business policy for the Government-for the late govern-

Supply-Railivays and Canals
ment or for this Government-to place orders for rails or any other materials or equipment required for these railways in order to relieve unemployment, if that means that higher prices have to be paid and charged against the railways. And I serve fair warning now upon the Minister of Railways that I reserve the right to criticise in the freest possible manner that method of conducting the business of our National Railways.
I have always maintained in this House and in the country that the operation of our National Railways should be placed on a sound business basis. I believe it can be done. But it cannot be done if unsound business practice is allowed! to govern. It should be left entirely with the management and the directors to decide where these purchases shall be made, and when. The-Government and the Minister of Railways occupy a very influential position, and it is the most natural thing in the world that even the management or the board of directors of the National Railways would pay attention to suggestions made by the minister as to where and when orders should be placed. Therefore it lies with the Minister of Railways and with the Government more than with any one else to absolutely dissociate the administration of these railways from considerations of this nature.
I inquired a little while ago from the minister what these rails would cost if they were purchased now, and I am sorry that he could not give me the information. I trust that before the main estimates of the Railway Department come down the minister will be able to furnish it. I was told-I do not know with what truth-that when these orders were placed last October they could have been placed at a cheaper rate. As I say, I do not know if my information is accurate. But before I take my seat I repeat once more that this is the only consideration that should govern in the administration of these National Railways, that the things necessary for their operation, the repair of cars and other rolling stock, the purchase of equipment, rails, ties and everything else, should be purchased on strict business methods by buying always where they can buy to the best advantage.

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
I would assure my hon.
friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar), that I do not think the conditions existing in Sydney differ very much from the conditions existing among the wheat-growers
in the western provinces. Some years ago they were very prosperous, they were receiving good prices for their wheat; and in the same way the steel workers were prosperous because the steel mills were busy and they were receiving good wages. We have an application before Parliament now for the establishment of a wheat board. I have no fault to find with that application; the western farmers have a perfect right to ask for it. But is that for the purpose of reducing the price of wheat to the growers of western Canada, or for the purpose of securing to them larger returns? If for the latter purpose, then surely the increased profit will have to come from those who consume the flour which is manufactured out of that western wheat.
No, no.

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip
speechtext: My hon. friends opposite say " no." I confess that I am not sufficiently familiar with the process by which they expect to get larger profits, but it always follows that if the producer of an article designs to get a higher price for it, then the consumer must pay more for the commodity.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip
speechtext: A wheat board was established a couple of years ago and the government financed its operations. I do not know if that is desired at the present time by the western provinces, but as I gathered from the discussion in this House some weeks ago it was the desire of our friends from the West to have a wheat board established whose operations would be financed out of the Treasury.
No, no.

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
The Government, of course, would not lose by doing so, because, as in the past, they would be recouped any moneys advanced. At all events, whether the particular details I refer to be correct or not, the fact is that conditions have arisen in western Canada which appear to make it necessary for our friends from the prairie provinces to take some further steps to secure better returns for the products of the wheat-growers. I did hear one hon. gentleman after another state in this House during the present session that wheat growing was most unprofitable for them owing to the small prices they received last year. That is perfectly true, and for my part I am prepared to support

Supply-Railways and Canals
any reasonable proposal that my hon. friends from the western provinces may present to this House for the purpose of ameliorating the condition of their constituents. Therefore I say it is unkind at least for my hon. friend from Marquette to object to a similar proposal, although in another form, which I am making in behalf of my constituents in the city of Sydney.

The member for Marquette has questioned the soundness of the business methods adopted by the late government last October. I am quite willing to take issue with him upon what was done from a business standpoint, and to permit the House to judge whether the business methods then adopted were sound or unsound. What was fundamental in the action of the government, and what that action was predicated upon, I submit was good business practice that was not uncommon during the past winter among private concerns.
First of all, we had a very serious unemployment situation. In the steel centres particularly where the car construction works were located it was the opinion not only of those in charge of the industry itself but of the municipalities that in no recent years were the prospects so serious for the working classes, and the government was petitioned time and again, and deputations from the municipal councils of those localities waited upon us to emphasize the seriousness of the situation.
Now, what did the government do? After conferring with the Department of Labour the government convinced itself that the conditions in the different localities, as represented by the municipal authorities, were very serious indeed and that the prospects for the winter season were absolutely hopeless for the working people. What the government did do was to confer with the representatives of the two boards in charge of the government lines as to the wisdom of placing orders for such supplies as would be used this spring and this season. Now, aside from the possible question of price, which has not been raised, I submit there is no bad business about that. The government ordered such rails as in the opinion of the boards would be required this season, and it was part of the arrangement that no payment was to be made until delivery was taken, and there was no obligation to take delivery before the rails were actually required. If it was bad business in the fall of 1921

to provide that these industries should operate during the winter season when it was most desirable, in the interests of the employees as well as of the country generally. that there should be employment, then I am quite willing to admit that my hon. friend from Marquette is right. But we acted as we deemed best; we took the responsibility then, and we stand by our action now. Why, it was not uncommon during the past season for those engaged in private industry, in manufacturing in many lines throughout Canada, to ask their customers to anticipate their requirements in order that the factories might be kept busy during the winter months when the really serious unemployment situation existed. If that was good business on the part of those engaged in pri-
9 p.m. vate enterprise, surely no question can be raised as to the action of the government with regard to the orders that were placed.

Will my hon. friend allow me a question I want to put to him with regard to the contracts for the repairs of cars? He says he wanted to relieve unemployment, but he took action which threw out a good many men in Truro, Halifax and Quebec, thus adding to the unemployment in our towns and cities.
The situation with reference to the repairing and rebuilding of cars rested on precisely the same basis as the placing of orders for rails.
You were wrong in both, then.

In the
placing of orders for rails and other supplies and for repairs to cars, the Government and the Department of Railways played no part at all.
I understood the hon. gentleman to say a few moments ago that neither the Government nor the railway management had anything to do with the placing of these contracts.
No, I said the Department of Railways.
And that the Minister of Labour had something to do with it.

The Minister of Labour was asked to confer with the boards of the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk in order that in placing the work regard should be had to the con-

dition of unemployment. There were also conferences between the executive heads of the two national systems and the Canadian Pacific, because in taking care of the unemployment situation it was necessary that the Canadian National board should know what the Canadian Pacific was doing in the matter of its commitments in respect of rails and cars. There were conferences,
I say, not only between the Department of Labour and the two boards of the National system, but between these two boards and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. My hon. friend referred to the placing of the cars and its effect upon the car works of the National system and of the Grand Trunk system. Well, that matter was fully considered by the boards; whether or not their judgment was correct is something that hon. members will themselves have to form an opinion upon. But the question of unemployment, in private industry as well as in the works of the companies themselves, was all canvassed. Whether or not the final decision was wise is something-
Will the ex-minister please make it quite clear whether it was the Gov-vernment that was advising the railway board or the railway board that was advising the Government?

It was a
matter upon which advice was unnecessary and was not given, so far as I know. If there was to be anticipation of the requirements of the road, it was necessary for the Government to make provision for the funds, and, in the Order in Council to which reference has been made, authority was given to the boards to anticipate the requirements that would result from the course that was to be taken.
When was that done?

Early in
October.
After dissolution?
After dissolution, yes. My hon. friend from Marquette has suggested that the transaction had some political significance.
Will the hon. gentleman deny that it had any political significance?

Absolutely
and positively. The fact that the dates synchronize does not involve that conclusion. My hon. friend who has just asked the question will not deny that the condition of unemployment existed. Surely he will not accuse the late government of
11, 1922
Supply-Railways and Canals
having brought about that condition because there was an election coming on and it might be considered expedient from a political point of view to give the orders.
If he does not go that far; if he admits that there was unemployment and that it was good business to give the orders, then his suggestion falls to the ground.
I do not admit anything.
I would not expect my hon. friend to do so.

I would like to ask the exMinister of Railways if he was aware that last fall, between the middle of October and the first of November, a train-load of new rails was shipped to the little town of Ste. Rose, presumably, I would say, to purchase a part of the Dauphin constituency for the government candidate. ___________________

I would
presume that my hon. friend would know sufficient about the policy under which our national roads are managed to find it unnecessary to ask the question, but as, apparently, it is necessary to make an explanation, let me say this: Under the law as it stands now, and as it stood in October of last year, neither the government, nor any .department of the government, has anything to do with the very condition which he states exists; and unless he suggests that the board of management of the road was operating the system and depositing the rails for political purposes his argument falls to the ground. Under the law as it stands, the government has absolutely nothing to do with the administration in the respect of which he has made this reference. Therefore I say that unless hon. gentlemen go the length of arguing that it was unsound business to attempt to take care of the unemployment situation, the action of the late government cannot be questioned. It did not require the expenditure of a single dollar prior to the time that it became necessary to take over these supplies for the purposes of the road. The car repairs were placed in such centres as was deemed wise. They were placed by the board of management of the road, not by the government, and they were pla'ced all over this country. Certain regard had to be paid to the question of the location of the industry concerned. That is, it would be impossible from a business point of view to take cars from western Canada to Nova Scotia to repair them. It would not
16DG

Supply-Railways and Canals
be considered good business to haul rails from Nova Scotia to the western provinces when those rails could be as well purchased at the Soo from the Algoma Steel company. All these were considerations which were dealt with by the board of management and in connection with which the government itself took no part directly or indirectly. That is the point I desire to stress-that the government had nothing in any way to do with these contracts, aside from supplying, or undertaking to supply, the money that would be necessary to anticipate these orders after the close of the fiscal year. Now that is the condition. As I stated before, if that is a matter as to which the late government should be censured then I assure you they are quite willing to take the censure.

I have been very
much surprised, as well as pleased, to hear the explanation given by the former Minister of Railways as to the letting of the car repairing contracts last fall, because this statement shows conclusively that I have been altogether misinformed on this question since I became Minister of Labour. For the first two or three months of this year I gave interviews to gentlemen, several of them, who forcibly indicated to me that all that was necessary ' to place an order for the repairing of cars of the National Railways, including the Grand Trunk, with their concern, was simply to make the necessary recommendation to my colleague the Minister of Railways. He, in turn would convey the view of the Minister of Labour to the operating officers of the railroads that such order was necessary to relieve unemployment in this centre or that centre and that any car repair order should go forward. I was given to understand that distinctly, and that is why I could not refrain from rising to say how pleased I am to receive the statement of the former Minister of Railways that these gentlemen who were coming to me for the first three months of this year were giving me entirely inaccurate information. Further, I understood the former Minister of Railways to suggest that it would not be good business to draw cars for repair from western Canada to eastern Canada. My information is-and I would like to be corrected if it is wrong-that Grand Trunk cars were hauled from a point west of Montreal to New Glasgow, Nova Scotia, a distance of about eight hundred miles, repaired and 
hauled back again. If that was not done I would like to have that inaccurate statement also corrected by the former Minister of Railways.
You are right.

I am very glad indeed to have had the explanation that has been given in regard to the letting of these car repairing contracts, because, I repeat, I was told it was done on the recommendation of the Minister of Labour, through the Minister of Railways, to the operating officers of the railroad.

I should like to say a few words in regard to the relief of unemployment that was assisted by the late government. I happen to be somewhat familiar with one section of this country anyway, that is the northern Ontario section, and I can say that the late government in that part of the province-the section in the neighbourhood Sault Ste. Marie and the section at the head of the lakes-did very much to relieve the unemployment just through such contracts as my hon. friend the late Minister of Railways has mentioned. I have no doubt at all that the present Minister of Labour has had many people call upon him for unemployment doles: I do not think that he has had any request from the head of the lakes for any assistance financially. There has been a certain amount of unemployment at the head of the lakes, but there has been very little in comparison with what there would have been had the late government not given instructions for the repair of government railway cars in that district. That is also true of Sault Ste. Marie because of the rail contracts that were given there.
Now, in regard to hauling cars eight hundred miles for repairs, I do not pretend to know anything about railway matters at all; but I do know that cars are often hauled eight hundred miles for that purpose. Many of the cars which are repaired by the Canada Car Company at the head of the lakes are hauled eight hundred miles from the prairie provinces, and a great many more than that distance. They come down loaded with wheat. Even though they do require repairs, their injuries, I take it, are not so great as to prevent them still remaining in use as rolling stock. They come down a great deal farther than eight hundred miles and are repaired, as I say, in the Canada Car Works; and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company does the same thing with its cars.

Supply-Railways and Canals
As a matter of fact the Canadian Pacific Railway Company-which we very often boast about as the greatest and most efficient corporation in the country-often gives contracts to the Canada Car Company, and the cars are of the same type

cars which have been used for carrying wheat from the prairie provinces, and many of them travelling much more than eight hundred miles to be repaired. So far as I am concerned-and I had something to do with the policy and saw something of it-I believe that the late government deserves a great deal of credit for the contracts they gave. If those contracts happened to be awarded before the election, was that any reason why the late government should ignore the unemployment conditions and not give them. Certainly not, to my mind.
Will my hon. friend tell me how many cars were repaired at Fort William?

I do not happen to have the figures, but I know there are still about five hundred men working in the car plant turning out that order, and that it is helping to relieve the unemployment conditions there.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Has not the late Minister of Railways just stated that the Government did not give these contracts?

I do not care anything about who gave the contracts. We are speaking about contracts given either by the Government, or by the government railways, for the repair of cars. I do not know who gave the contracts. I had nothing to do with that; I was not Minister of Railways. But I know that government railway cars were repaired at the head of the lakes, and I repeat it had much to do with relieving the unemployment situation in northern Ontario

that work and the contracts which were obtained by the steel mills at Sault Ste. Marie.
Now, in regard to the remarks by my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) who speaks of desiring the greatest efficiency on the part of the government railways. I doubt if there is an hon. member here who does not wish to see that. But at the same time, if a government road contract for the repair of cars, or the repair of something else, or the manufacture of rolling stock, or the manufacture of rails, can be given in such a manner that it helps to relieve the unemployment situation in this country, whether given by
the late government or the present Government, so far as I am concerned, even if it can be shown that it costs a little more-unless the cost is so much more that it is a disgrace-I will promise the present Government that I will support them in such a contract.
Another remark of the hon. leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Crerar) was rather a criticism of the steel bonus. I remember when the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) was citicised on other occasions in regard to this steel bonus which he brought in, when previously in office, I have seen him rise to his feet on some occasions and prove, and I think conclusively, that this bonus was a fine piece of legislation. I notice that when the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) raises the same cry, the Minister of Finance does not rise, I presume for-the reason-that it is not good policy, in the present condition of the Government, to quarrel with the hon. member for Marquette. I am going to help out the Minister of Finance in that matter, because I agree with the policy he introduced in 1896, or about that time. I think I am correct in saying that the bounties were brought in by the present Minister of Finance when he was in the Liberal government of that time. He brought in bounties which amounted to some millions of dollars. The hon. member for Marquette gave some figures which, I think, are approximately correct, as to the amount paid on these bounties. I have looked into the question myself, because, as some hon. members of this House know, I gave on occasions various discourses on the iron question in this country, and I considered the iron and steel question at some length. I heard the hon. Minister of Finance state, and I agree with him, that due to these bounties to a great extent the steel and iron manufacturing plants of this country were built up. The steel and iron industries were built up to a great extent by the very bounties given about 1896 by the present Minister of Finance who was a member of the former Liberal government. Possibly they were put on just before, but I think it was about that time. In my opinion these bounties had very much to do with building up the iron and steel manufacturing processes of this country. I wish to compliment the present Minister of Finance upon having kept them in force as long as he did. For some years past they have been discontinued.

Supply-Railways and Canals
I notice that my hon. friend from Marquette and many of his friends cheered him strongly when he criticized these bounties. I hold the Estimates in my hand, and in the Estimates I find a figure of $6,084,000 in the agricultural estimates. Last year it was $5,900,000. I challenge my hon. friends to my left to show that this $6,000,000 item is not a bounty to the agricultural interests of this country when the money is paid. I challenge them to say that it is not practically a direct bounty. In the agricultural estimates I find these items: Experimental Farm, $1,315,000; Administration and enforcement of the Destructive Insect and Pest Act, $235,000: Health of Animals, administration and enforcement of the Animal Contagious Diseases, and Meat and Canned Food Acts, $1,710,000, and so on, and all these items make a total of over $6,000,000. If that is not a direct assistance to the agricultural interests, I do not know what it is. It does not assist me as a professional man, and it does not assist manufacturing or any other interests. It is certainly a direct assistance to the agricultural interest, and therefore it is a bounty to that interest. So far as I am concerned, I support it, and support it whole-heartedly, and I think it should be carried out. But I think the members of the agricultural section of this House should be consistent when they criticise bounties, and if they are going to absolutely condemn all bounties in their criticisms in this House, then they should go after the agricultural bounty in the present estimates.

I wish to ask a question, which perhaps is not in order, but the hon. gentleman referred to the votes for the administration and enforcement of the Destructive Insect and Pest Act, Health of Animals, administration and enforcement of the Animal Contagious Diseases, and Meat and Canned Food Acts, and so on. I would like to know how the hon. member could call that a bonus to the agricultural interest. As a matter of fact, it is due to a large extent-
Order, order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I draw the attention of the committee to the fact that this is getting almost beyond the bounds of order, because the particular item deals with the expenditure in connection with rails and so on, $735,000, and while it is quite possible to make comparisons, such as were made by the hon. gentleman from Marquette, it is

getting now beyond the bounds of relevancy to this particular item.
I think so.

I think the Chairman is quite right. I shall apply anything I have to say to the item under discussion. I wish to say that when you help to relieve unemployment, as is requested by my hon. friend from Cape Breton South (Mr. Kyte), who asks that work under this item be performed in the steel mills in his constituency, it is reasonable to do so, even if that work does cost this country a little more than it costs in some other plant. Is it not better for this country that we should pay a few more dollars that way, than that we should hand out doles, as a charity, to the unemployed of this country? I certainly think it is, and I am perfectly in accord with the request of the hon. member for Cape Breton South, when he requests that the steel mills should, if possible, if the expense be not too great, be kept in employment in times such as these. I say that, perhaps, with a certain amount of selfishness, because, if the unemployment became very bad in New Ontario, I should certainly be one of the first to request that the New Ontario corporations should be assisted in the same way to prevent unemployment continuing. I should like to have dealt with one or two other remarks of the hon. member for Marquette, but seeing that objection is taken, I think I shall have to refrain at the present time.

It is not my intention to enter into a discussion of the bounty question to-night, because I think you had good reason to declare it out of order. The proper time for this discussion will be the budget debate. There is, however, a very important question before this committee to-night in connection with this item, and that is: Are the Canadian National Railways administered by the Canadian National Railway Board, or were they administered by the late government on the eve of the last general election for political purposes? The ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Stewart) tells us he and his government had absolutely nothing to do with the sending of a train load of rails to a certain constituency on the eve of the election, and I think, in giving that answer, he was perfectly right in theory. But if he was right in theory in giving that answer, was the late government right in deciding where these orders were to be placed? "Oh, but," he said, "there were a great many

Supply-Railways and Canals
private corporations who did absolutely the same thing, who placed orders for goods they did not need, in order to relieve unemployment." I sat in this House during the last session, and if I remember rightly,
I heard a great deal about unemployment and about the methods employed by the late government to relieve that condition. During the recess I heard a great deal about unemployment, but the government made no move in the way of giving orders until the month of October, after the general election had been announced, and when it was once more seeking the support of the people of Canada. Then they thought of unemployment, and what did they do? They passed an Order in Council authorizing a member of their government, the Minister of Labour, to put the gun to the head of the administrators of the Canadian National Railways and tell them when and where they should get their cars repaired, and when and where they should buy their rails. The ex-Minister of Railways said that private corporations did the same thing, but I should like him to name one private corporation that purchased goods from other similar corporations when its own shops were closed and its own employees were going without labour and without food. It is well known that the Canadian government railway shops at St. Malo, while they were, perhaps, not completely dosed, were working on very short time with a greatly reduced staff. The Grand Trunk shops in the city of Montreal were working on short time with a reduced staff. The shops at FraserviTle were working on short time with a reduced staff, and at Moncton the same state of affairs existed. What happened? Was employment given to their own men? Did they prevent their own machinery from being ruined 'by rust and neglect? Did they endeavour t,o use it by giving employment to their own men? Not at all. They closed up their own shops and they gave work to other firms. They did that by Order in Council. What right did the late government have to decide by Order in Council where the work should be done? If the late government desired to operate the National Railways of Canada and were brave and courageous enough to say so, well and good; but that is not what they pretended. They told us in the last Parliament that they had absolutely nothing to do with the National Railways. When they were asked an ordinary question concerning disbursements, or the cost of coal, or supplies, or rails, or cars, they said; We do not know
anything about that. We will ask Mr. Hanna in Toronto. We cannot give you an answer; we have no right to give you an answer. We have nothing to do with the administration of these roads. 'They maintained that attitude until Parliament had been dissolved, until the candidates of all political parties were before their electors, and then they decided to change all this and pass Orders in Council to oblige Mr. Hanna and his associates to place their orders just exactly where the government would decide.
It may be argued that an Order in Council was necessary to provide the funds. There was no Order in Council passed to provide the funds in the month of October last. A Governor General's Warrant was passed, on the 21st December, 1921, to pay the debts contracted just a few days before the late government laid down the reins of office. The first Order in Council was passed in order to enable the then Minister of Labour to wield the big stick we heard so much about the other night, and to tell the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways where those orders would be given. The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) said that he would support this Government if it did the same thing. I should like to ask him if he woulld support this Government, if it took damaged cars from his constituency, from the other side of Fort William, and brought them to St. Malo, in the province of Quebec, to have them repaired, while his own shops were biased or running on short time.

Speaking generally, I would not; tout the question depends a little on unemployment conditions at the time. I know nothing about the St. Malo shops; but I repeat what I said a few minutes ago; I do .know that whatever contracts were given in northern Ontario, which is a part of the Country I am most familiar with, did a great dCal to relieve the situation of unemployment and were very badly needed.

Exactly. The action
taken toy the late government on the eve of the election relieved unemployment where they wanted to relieve it and created unemployment where they wanted it to be created, or where they did not care whether it was created or not.
Mr. MANION; Would it not be a rather peculiar thing if they relieved unemployment where they did not want to relieve it?

Supply-Railivays and Canals

It would have been a very peculiar thing, but not half so peculiar as many things accomplished by the late government. My closing remarks are that from the explanations of the ex-Minister of Railways-and I may be very dense- I have not yet been able to understand why an Order in Council was necessary. I have not yet understood why a government, that had nothing to do with the administration of the National Railways, could empower a Minister of Labour by Order in Council to direct where this work should be done, and I have yet to learn that it is good policy for any corporation to close its own shops and use its money to have its work performed by other institutions while its own machinery and employees are absolutely idle.

The hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Boivin) has expressed very great surprise that the late government found it necessary to pass an Order in Council in order to determine where certain car repairs should be carried on. No such Order in Council was passed; no Order in Council was ever passed directing where any work would be done. He also expresses very great surprise that an Order in Council should have been passed by the late government providing that the Minister of Railways should wield the big stick-

I said, the Minister of Labour.
Mr. STEWART (Lanark) that the Minister of Labour should wield the big stick and direct the officers of the two railway boards where the cars were to be repaired. No such Order in Council was ever passed, and there was no Order in Council giving to the Minister of Labour the right to determine where# the work should be done.
What did he have to do with the matter then?

He had
nothing further to do with it than was authorized in the Order in Council itself-
Hear. hear.
-to confer with the representatives of the boards.
Oh, oh.

It seems
remarkable that hon. gentlemen should be so much amused that, in the consideration of the question of unemployment, the

Minister of Labour and the Labour Department should be brought into consultation. The whole question of the placing of orders, of the number of cars to be repaired, of the number of rails to be ordered, was one with which the late government, neither directly nor indirectly, had any voice. I should like to make that clear.
Except the Minister of Labour.
The Minister of Labour had absolutely nothing to do with it.
What did he do then to relieve unemployment?

If my hon. friend is not able to grasp the situation, I am afraid I cannot help him. Neither the late government nor the late Minister of Labour had a single thing to say or had any voice in the question of what cars were to be repaired, what supplies were to be purchased. That was a matter that was entirely within the jurisdiction of the two boards. Let there be no mistake about that. No attempt was made on behalf of the government to influence either board in any direction.
The hon. member said a moment ago that the Minister of Labour was to confer with someone or another with reference to the expenditure of this money. With whom was he to confer?
Possibly I would make myself clear to the committee if I said this, that the Minister of Labour was to be the source of information as to the question of unemployment in the country.
To whom was that information to be given?

That information was to 'be available for the members of the two boards of the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk, in whose hands the whole question of the placing of these orders and the purchase of supplies rested.
Why was that included in the Order in Council?
Why was what included?

The fact that the Minister of Labour should advise.

Supply-Railways and Canals
Because the whole situation was 'predicated on unemployment.
So that it was included in the Order in Council.

Yes. The Minister of Labour could not direct where a single order should go. He could give to the officials of the two boards the information as to unemployment which goes to the department and is on record there.
Will my hon. friend tell me whether the Minister of Labour at the time advised the board of the Canadian National Railways as to where there was unemployment to be relieved?

I have no knowledge of that: I never was present.
Some non. MEMBERS: Oh, oh.
Hon. gentlemen laugh; tout I would ask them in what respect it would be possible for me to have the information which my hon. friend has just asked for?
It should be possible, because you were Minister of Railways.

The Minister of Railways, under the law as it stands and as it stood then, has absolutely no authority to place orders for supplies. Surely my hon. friend know? that. That was the condition in October of last year, and it is the condition to-day.
Can my hon. friend explain why 100 men were discharged at Fraser-ville when there was unemployment there, while unemployment was relieved elsewhere?

And 300 in Quebec
city?

I am afraid I cannot make the matter clearer to my hon. friend. If unemployment existed in the industries that were owned by the government, that was something of which the government had no notice; and I know that in the placing of all orders consideration was taken of the whole question of unemployment, not only in connection with the industries owned and operated by the government, but throughout the country as well. With regard to the question of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) as to whether or not the late Minister of Railways knew that cars were taken from Montreal to Nova Scotia to be repaired, I
do understand that cars were taken from the province of Quebec to Nova Scotia to be rebuilt, and they were taken there for two reasons: first, because some of the car companies, not only in the province of Quebec, but also some in Nova Scotia, were not equipped for the handling of the class of work that was to toe done; and, secondly, because at that particular time the condition of unemployment was much more severe in some centres of the province of Nova Scotia than in Montreal, where the work might have been done had it been done in the province of Quebec.
And the relief in Nova Scotia served a more useful purpose.
The minister has given two reasons. I might add a third: Colonel Cantley was a Tory candidate.
That is a matter which the member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) will have to thresh out with the boards of the two lines who placed the order.

Colonel Cantley was a
member of the board.
That is a matter that does not go to the *oot of the whole question, for the reason-
And he was defeated too.
-that the department did not place the wder.
That ord' r went to grease the wheels, so to speak.

!l wish to make one further reference to what was said by the Minister of Labour, who referred to the placing of orders through the Minister of Railways. If I understood him aright that is what he told the House.

What I said was that the impression had been conveyed to me repeatedly during the first two or three months I was in office, by representatives of these car concerns, that all previous orders for the repair of cars at New Glasgow, Amherst, Montreal, Hamilton and Fort William, had been m '^e as the result of recommendations made by the Minister of Labour, as to the unemployment situation in the particular localities. Those recommendations were made through the Minister of Railways to the officers of the boards of directors of the National railways, and the orders went forth ac-

Supply-Railways and Canals
cordingly. I was given to understand that all that was necessary was for me to realize the unemployment situation in the various localities interested in the matter, and to make the necessary recommendations to the Minister of Railways, and that he would pass the word along to the board of directors, who would be only too glad to place another order for the repairs of additional cars, if we had additional cars to repair.

I desire to state without any qualification that all that was said to my hon. friend the Minister of Labour as to what took place last fall is entirely without foundation in fact. I have no mental reservations on the matter. I declare that his statement with reference to what took place has absolutely no foundation in fact at all.

I desire to speak on this matter only because it seems to me that there is a considerable amount of misinformation, not only on the part of hon. members directly opposite, but on this side of the House as well. In the first place, it is admitted to-day by the best railway concerns on this continent that it is not a paying proposition for railways to repair their own cars. In the United States there is not a single big concern to-day that does so. In Buffalo and in other parts of the United States there are large car repairing plants that do this sort of work, not for the government, but for private railway systems in that country. As regards this order that was placed by the late government and which is being completed at the present time, I would venture to say that in the Canada Car and Foundry Company's shops in Amherst the repairs have been made at 30 per cent less than they could be done in the government shops in any part of the Canadian National Railway system.
What about the Canadian Pacific railway?

They are also giving out work for repairs. Now, what are the facts? I am not here to discuss whether or not this order was given with a view to political effect. If it was, they made a mess of it, because they did not get to work until about three days before the election. As I say, I know not what the idea was from the political standpoint; but I do know that if ever there was a government or a railway board that was justified

in giving work to car companies in Amherst and New Glasgow, that government existed last October. I say this in justice to these towns, although possibly the statement may not be popular on this side of the House. In the town of Amherst, in which I live when at home, there are ordinarily employed in the different industries 2,300 men. Last fall out of those 2,300 workmen less than 400 had employment. For some months the local car works, which had employed from 1,000 to 1,250 men, were absolutely idle; men walked the streets; women were suffering; children were in want; the town itself spent large sums of money in attempting to deal with the situation; a relief association was formed and distributed thousands of dollars collected from the people; the red cross society endeavoured to cope with the situation. This order for five hundred cars was a godsend to the town.

Does my hon. friend realize
that the criticism directed against the late government was not because they gave a car order to Amherst to relieve unemployment, but because they delayed doing so until the election campaign began, granting relief only when they thought it might be useful to them?

I am not here to tell
my hon. friend or anyone else what was in the mind of the late government. I am reciting the condition of affairs that existed in Amherst at that time, a condition which demanded immediate relief, and I am only saying that the best managed railroads throughout this continent are adopting this particular principle of placing their cars for repairs in outside shops. I am also pointing out that the government would have been derelict in its duty if it had not come to the rescue of the unemployed in Amherst last fall; there is no question about that.
Someone has said that certain Grand Trunk cars were brought down to New Glasgow for repair. Why? Because they were steel cars which could not be repaired anywhere else, as the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Stewart) stated to-niglff
Let me now speak particularly to my hon. friends directly opposite. We expect this fall the greatest crop that western Canada has ever produced. We all pray that it may be so. There are to-day on the government-owned roads and roads controlled by the government about 15,000 cars needing repairs. Suppose there is a

Supply-Railways and Canals
bumper crop in the West this fall, do you not think that any government should be reprimanded that did not put those cars in proper order to move that crop? Why should not the Government place those cars in the repair shops and relieve unemployment?
At what date was unemployment felt for the first time in Amherst?
About fifteen years ago we had unemployment.
At what time did the late government start relief there?

It was about fifteen years ago that we first had unemployment in Amherst, and then the government of my late lamented chief, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, placed contracts with the Robb Engineering Works for the repair of locomotives, to relieve the situation. That was the precedent which was established for putting work in private shops. I believe that the late government was not only justified in placing this order, but I also believe that it is the absolute duty of the present Government to relieve by similar means the unemployment situation existing in these towns to-day.

Would the hon. gentlemen tell the committee if in his opinion the law as it stands to-day permitted the late government, or permits this Government, to dictate to the management of the Canadian National Railways where they shall place orders for the repair of cars?

I do not think that question is relevant to this discussion. If I did think so I would say that as the Government owns 22,000 miles of railways, and has the right to do anything for the relief of unemployment, it is its duty to take such action as may be necessary to that end. I may be defending the action of the late government.
Oh, oh.
Does my hon. friend believe that the late government should have started before dissolution to relieve unemployment?
A lPtle bit sooner.
Unemployment was not acute in Amherst until about August of last year. Let us be honest in this matter now. That is when unemployment became acute.
You said it began ten years ago.	*

I said that unemployment became acute in August of last year; but in order to satisfy my hon. friend that we had a precedent for what was done by the late government, I reminded him that some years ago the government of the late Sir Wilfri'd Laurier awarded contracts for the repair' of locomotives in Amherst when there was unemployment there, although unemployment was not acute at that time.
I do not think that our friends opposite should take the view which they do upon this question, because they may need these very cars within a few months, and we all hope they will. If it is true that there are 15,000 cars which need to be repaired, and if there is unemployment in this country, I think that a government instead of handing out doles here and there should give work to these men, who do not want charity but wages.
A good deal has been said to-night as to unemployment at Moncton, Fraserville and other places. I do not know the condition of affairs except in Moncton, and I deny that there was unemployment at Moncton at the time or that a single workman was displaced by giving this order to the Canadian Car and Foundry Company to relieve unemployment in Amherst. There is not the slightest doubt that an emergency existed in that town and that the relief was absolutely necessary.

Considerable criticism
has been levelled against the late government for having placed certain orders last fall for steel rails and other equipment in order to relieve unemployment. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) has described much more forcibly than I can the conditions prevailing in some of our industrial centres last fall. If some hon. gentlemen who have been criticising the action of the government at that time could have seen those conditions, I do not think they would be so ready to condemn the course that was then taken in placing orders in anticipation of our rail requirements in order that employment might be given to our workmen during the winter months.
The hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) asked when the unemployment commenced. I may say that strong representations were made to the managements of the railway companies last spring by representatives of the steel companies at

Supply-Railways and Canals
Sydney and Sault Ste. Marie to place railway business in.order to provide employment for the men during the summer season. Accordingly, the orders were placed; they were completed in the fall, and the men were faced with unemployment in the winter. It was only natural, therefore, that the Minister of Labour should suggest to the railway companies that they should anticipate their requirements in the matter of rails and place orders so as to provide against unemployment. That is what was done. It is said that this course was adopted for political purposes. Well, so far as rail orders were concerned, at any rate, if it was adopted for that purpose it did not have the desired effect, because the greater portion of the rail orders were given to the mills at Sydney. What was the result? The hon. member for Cape Breton asked the Minister of Railways to have the managements of the railways anticipate their requirements to provide against the unemployment that has been existing down there for some time. I quite sympa-
10 p.m. thize with him in the situation that he finds there. But let me tell you how the steel company in the constituency that I represent took care of the business that was given to them last fall. They realized that if they worked on full shift they could turn the order out in a very short time, and that the men would again be out of employment; so they put the mill on single shift and were thus able, on the business which they got at that time, to keep the wheels turning until about the middle of April. They sustained a loss of over half a million dollars in their endeavour to play fair with the companies that gave them the orders and with the men whom they employed. Is it not much better that the management of the government railways should anticipate their needs in this regard than that they should hand out large sums of money to relieve distress and suffering throughout the country, as the Department of Labour has had to do? You find in the estimates appropriations for over $500,000 to be paid out for relief

practically charity. The men do not want that; all they are asking for is an opportunity to work to earn an honest living for themselves.
Apparently the hon. member for Marquette does not think very kindly of the steel companies in this country; he criticises severely the subsidies or bounties granted to them in order that they might become established. While he is correct

in stating that the bounties amounted to some $15,000,000, I may say that four of the largest steel companies in Canada have paid back to the Dominion treasury, through the medium of customs taxes on machinery and supplies, more than they received from the Government by way of bounties. The Algoma Steel Corporation in Sault Ste. Marie has a pay roll of approximately $8,000,000 a year. Think of the immense amount of tonnage that is provided for the National railways as a result of the operations of that corporation. Think of the amount of money that is collected by way of income tax upon the salaries of their officials and some of their better paid employees. When these things are taken into consideration, the amount paid by way of bounties is very small indeed, compared with the return that has been made to the public treasury. Moreover, when war broke out and Canada was asked to make munitions, we were able to do it only because we had the steel companies to take up this work. The hon. member for Marquette is very critical when it comes to the matter of bounties, but he is not so critical of the amounts found in the estimates to provide relief to needy settlers in Alberta and Saskatchewan by way of necessary supplies, wood, clothing, fuel, etc., and fodder for their animals. The amount provided for that purpose this year is $325,000, and a similar amount was voted last year. I do not criticise that at all, but is it not better for the government railways to anticipate their needs and thus provide work for the unemployed, than to hand out doles and charities?
Was any unemployment relieved in my hon. friend's riding?

Unemployment certainly was relieved in my riding and in the city of Sault Ste. Marie as the result of rail orders placed. No part of the $500,000 that is to toe passed by this House for the purposes of relief is going to Sault Ste. Marie,
[DOT]-due to the fact that this rail order was placed.
The other day the hon. member for Marquette pleaded eloquently against the appointment by the Government of a special railway committee, to consider the question of freight rates, but suggested that the Crowsnest pass agreement toe allowed to again come into effect. He realizes that our railways have to be run on a business basis and that a proper schedule of rates must be maintained if increased deficits

Supply-Railways and Canals
are to be avoided; yet he asks for the restoration of the Crowsnest pass agreement in July, the effect of which would be materially to reduce the earning power of the national railways and to confer the greatest proportion of benefit on the shippers of grain in the West. Why, then, should he object when it is suggested that rail orders should be placed in advance to provide for unemployment, thus avoiding the necessity of handing out large sums for the purposes of relief?

Now that the oratorical
contest is ended, I would like to speak on behalf of the few in this corner of the House who still survive and who are fearful of a second attack. I would like to ask the minister how much of this money spent on car repairing was expended in the city of Winnipeg, and in the town of Transcona, where the government shops are located, and where the men were working on short time throughout the months already referred to in this debate? I put this question because I would like the people of these constituencies to know the extent to which the government came to their relief at that time when unemployment was rampant. I cannot see why my constituency should be discriminated against in favour of the constituency represented by my hon. friend from Fort William and Rainy River.

Before that question is answered may I point out one little fact to my hon. friend on my left-this is just for the information of the committee. While a contract was given for the repairing of cars in Fort William-I forgot to mention the fact before-the work on that contract was not done until one month after the election was over. That may answer my hon. friend's question. It did not have very much to do with the election apparently. If there had been a desire to influence the election the work would have begun one month at least before the election was over.
That is not a reply to my question.
In reply to my hon. friend, as regards the 2,000 cars mentioned in the Order in Council under discussion no orders were placed in the city of Winnipeg.

I would like to make one suggestion. If the Government have discovered any irregularities in connection with this matter on the part of the former government, they should make a charge to that effect publicly and follow it to a logical conclusion. The discussion on this matter for political reasons does not seem to get us anywhere whatsoever.
I would suggest that the Government should do that and then let us pass the estimate and get on with business in view of the fact that so much time has already been spent in the discussion of this matter.
Item agreed to.

I want to make a suggestion. It has already been stated by the ex-Minister of Railways that the practice has been followed of giving orders and making no payments until deliveries have been made. Now, I do think we must have some regard for conditions of unemployment, and I want to suggest that possibly orders can be given without specifying any prices, and that the prices to be paid finally when delivery is made be competitive prices. In that way our railways in the country will be protected against any kind of loss.
I did not have the opportunity of being present-
