Staff and repairs-further amount required, $91,000.

I want to correct a wrong impression in the mind of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). He did not hear the rather animated discussion before he entered the Chamber, or he would not be labouring under a misapprehension, as he appears to be doing just now. No one from the West, or from any other part of Canada, as far as I know, is objecting to having cars repaired.
Where are you going to repair them?

They should be repaired wherever they can be repaired to best advantage. We have repair shops attached to the Canadian National Railways. I submit that, when we have plants for the repairing of these cars, our own plants should have the opportunity of repairing them. I know it was argued by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan)-probably with a good deal of reason; I do not know-that in the United States the railways are giving their repair works out to private corporations. That may be. I am not discussing that aspect of the question. The point that I endeavoured to bring out earlier in the evening is that it is not a sound business policy to let contracts for the purpose of relieving unemployment at higher costs or higher prices than would otherwise obtain.
They were not let at other prices than would otherwise obtain.
That information has yet to be disclosed.

Does the hon. gentleman suggest that the contracts that >
were given last fall were at a higher price than would otherwise obtain?

My hon. friend, the exMinister of Railways (Mr. Stewart) appears unduly sensitive in respect to this. My remarks earlier in the evening were in response to the remarks of my hon. friend from Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Kyte) in which he argued that it would be sound policy for this Government to borrow money, build cars, make rails and store them up against the future.
I submit that is not a sound policy, and it was against that principle of doing business in connection with our national railways that I was protesting and that I still protest. It is not sound business. Our National Railways are operating under a great handicap. We have deficits in operation. We are unable to meet our fixed charges. We have a constant stream of criticism coming from those who are opposed to government ownership of these railways, and we have the railways, not by virtue of our belief in the principle of public ownership, but because of the absolute and complete breakdown of private ownership. Now when we have them, let us handle them in a business way. That is all I am pleading for or suggesting. I am not suggesting, and no one is suggesting, that we should go along without making the necessary repairs to cars and engines, but I maintain it should be done according to sound business practice.

Does my hon. friend want to continue paying in the shops the McAdoo award wages, which are a great deal higher than are paid in the ordinary steel industries of this country, where steel cars are repaired? They are paying higher wages in the United States and cars are repaired at a much greater cost than when we have the arrangement for the repairs of cars on the cost plus basis. But that is not the policy he suggests. It is all very well to talk of repair shops at all points of the Canadian National railways. He has not the slightest conception in regard to the repair shop. There is not a repair shop on the Canadian National where they can repair a steel car, which is the modern car used in the transportation of freight in this country, and, therefore, it was wise and sound policy to send the steel cars to be repaired at these places where steel cars are made, and steel cars are not made in any shop that belongs to the Canadian National railways. It was sound and wise policy to have cars repaired on the basis of cost plus, rather than to pay the McAdoo award wages and the Chicago award wages in the ordinary shops of the country. That is the position of the matter. Moreover, in a very great number of cases the repairs could not be made in the ordinary repair shops. I say, instead of giving grants to municipalities, on the basis of one-third of the expenditure being made by the municipality for the purpose of relieving unemployment it is better to undertake work of this kind having regard to the fact that these cars supply the transportation necessities of the country. It is not sound business policy

Supply-Railways and Canals
to allow these cars to remain unrepaired, or, if you are going to repair them, to repair them at a higher cost than the amount which you could have them repaired for on a business basis, and thus allow the railway to deteriorate, instead of endeavouring to keep the railway up to date. Is it not better to buy those things which are essential to the operation of a government railway system, and have them on hand, and by this means prevent unemployment, than to give money for which there is no return, on the basis of a one-third contribution by the municipality?

I have no particular
quarrel with the remarks of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). They do not conflict with anything I said a moment ago, or earlier in the debate. By all means have repair work done where it can be done most cheaply. I am suggesting to the Minister of Railways that the Board of Directors of the National railways should do that very thing. If there is only one repair shop in which they can repair steel cars, they will have to go there. I can tell the hon. member that, as far as western , Canada is concerned, there are tens of thousands of cars hauling grain and not one of them is a steel car. At the very time when the unemployment question was very serious, and the orders were placed last autumn for the relief of unemployment, there was not a single car sent to Trans-cona shops, which are situated a few miles from Winnipeg, where millions of dollars have been spent in establishing a car plant for the National railways. I really think that the hon. member for Pictou has not caught the sense of my remark, and I have no quarrel with what he said.

The only difference between the hon. member and myself is that apparently he wants to have the cars repaired at Transcona. There is a car shop there, and he thinks they should all be taken to that shop, although he does not know whether they can repair them there or not. If they do not go there, does he . object to cars in eastern Canada going to Shops which are quite handy, if they can be repaired at a less cost than in the other shops?
Not at all.
The hon. gentleman agrees with me.

Certainly.
[ Mr. Macdonald. ]

I desire to make one explanation which, I think, will enlighten the House as to the way in which these cars are repaired.. I regret very much, if this matter is to be disicussed, that we have not before us the contracts made by the late government, or by the Railway Board, with the different companies. I wish to say that these cars are not dealt with exactly on what we call the cost plus basis. The contract was made that the government was to pay the car companies for their labour, plus a certain small percentage, but as far as all supplies for those cars are concerned, the Government itself, or the Canadian National Board, has the right to supply every article that is required in this work, and if it is not considered that the price being charged by the company for its supplies is reasonable, it will not pay that company for those supplies, if it can show that they could have been bought for a less price elsewhere. So that it is not only a contract on the usual cost plus basis, but it is even a better contract than that, because it is only the labour cost plus.

While we are talking about car repairs, I desire to offer a suggestion to the Minister of Railways. Being an old railroad man myself, when I am travelling on the Canadian National railway system, it is always a pleasure to me and, in fact, second nature, to chat with railroad men. I have asked them this question:	Why do we have so many
wrecks on the Canadian National Railways? I give this to the Minister; I do not know how true it is; but they tell me that the reason is that American railways ship their old cars, loaded, of course, to Canada. These cars, which are in bad condition when they cross the border, are accepted, and shortly afterwards in Canadian territory, a journal or something else will break, and that will cause a wreck. The railway men tell me that these ears have to be repaired at the expense of the Canadian railways before they are sent back to the United States. I merely offer the suggestion to the minister that, I think, the inspection of these cars before they enter Canadian territory should be very severe.

I rise, not for the purpose
of entering into a discussion of the matter before the committee, nor to criticise the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Stewart), nor to come to his defence as regards contracts let for the repair of cars during the

Supply-Railways and Canals
late campaign. I feel it is my duty to correct an erroneous impression that may have been given to the committee in regard to the railway shops in the city of Moncton. When the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) says that there is not, in the Dominion of Canada, a railway shop connected with the Canadian National Railways that is in a position to repair steel cars, I can only say that he is altogether mistaken as regards the magnificent shops in the city of Moncton belonging to the National Railway system. If my hon. friend has any doubt in his mind or fails to accept my word in regard to the matter, all he has to do is to drop off at that city, and he will see steel cars being repaired there every day of the year.
I also desire to correct an error that was made by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan). I only wish his remarks were absolutely correct. I understood him to say that one of the reasons why the cars were-and should have been-repaired at Amherst and New Glasgow was the extreme unemployment situation ip Amherst, while not a single man was out of employment in Moncton. I only wish the facts had been as stated by the hon. member; but I would draw to his attention this fact-and I know no one understands it more clearly than the ex-Minister of Railways-that last summer between six and seven hundred employees of the Canadian National Railways were laid off in the shops in the city of Moncton, and only a small percentage of that number have been reinstated.
I rise only for the purpose of correcting those two errors that have been made by my hon. friends from Nova Scotia, and I would point out, for the information of the Minister of Railways and the committee, that, in the city of Moncton, we have, in connection with the Canadian National railway system, shops splendidly located, splendidly equipped and manned by employees who are absolutely competent and able to carry out, not only the repair of cars, but the building, construction and equipment of all classes of cars required for the Canadian National Railways.

A few minutes ago the Minister of Railways informed us that the price of steel rails was $49 or $50 a ton. The suggestion has been made by some hon. members that that price was not in accordance with the market. Was the price at which the rails were purchased in accordance with the market at the time?

One would
have gathered from the discussion this evening that I was not present when the order was placed, but I understood that the price at which it was placed was about the market price at the time. I promised the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Cre-rar) that I would give him some information upon that point, and I hope, when my main estimates come down, to be able to give my hon. friend the information that he desires.

I have endeavoured two or three times to get from the exMinister of Railways (Mr. Stewart) the exact meaning of his remarks in regard to the negotiations that took place between the then Minister of Railways and the railway management or the Government officials, or whoever these negotiations took place with. In view of the discussion that has taken place in this chamber to-night, I think it would be wise if we could have that Order in Council laid on the Table of the House so that we might understand exactly what its effect was.

I have not a copy of the Order in Council myself, but the minister or some other member of the Government can place it on the Table. There is nothing in that document that would justify the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite, or upon which, could rest the suspicion that appears to exist as regards the action on the part of the boards of the government railways and as regards the late government itself in permitting and authorising the action by the boards.

I have no suspicion at all. I simply want to find out the facts. I asked the hon. member twice, and I was unable to grasp, from the answers that he made, whom the then Minister of Railways had these negotiations with. If he can answer that question, probably we shall not need the Order in Council.

I have
stated several times, since this discussion started that, as regards the then Minister of Railways and any other official connected with the government, they played no part in the placing of these orders. That is surely an unqualified statement, and it is the fact.
That is the Department of Railways and Canals?

I am speaking now of the Department of Railways,

1710	,	,
Supply-Railways and Canals
because that is the official department having control of railway management. That department had nothing to do with placing the orders. The orders were placed by two boards as a result of conferences held between certain members of those boards, as I understand the matter and understand it still, and the Canadian Pacific Railway. The only connection between any government official and the boards in the consideration of the matter was that the Labour Department, through its minister, was the fount of information upon questions of unemployment upon which they might wish to secure information. The then Minister of Railways played no part in any connection further than to secure the authorization through Council of the necessary financial arrangements to give effect to what was decided upon. That is the whole story as regards the Department of Railways and the then government. I might qualify that by this, that when the petitions and memorials and all the other communications came to the department from municipalities in which unemployment was most severe-
Which department?
The Department of Railways. There is no question that we received petitions from municipalities, boards of trade, and labour organizations.	;
Why were these petitions sent to the Minister of Railways? Should they not, in the ordinary course, be addressed to the Minister of Labour?

'I do not know why they were sent to the Minister of Railways, but my hon. friend will bear me out when I say that there is generally throughout the country a great misconception as to the part which the Department of Railways plays in the actual management of the nationally owned railway system. That is a condition for which the late government was not responsible, and one for which this Government would not be responsible. There is a very large Volume of public opinion in this country that the Department of Railways and Canals plays a direct part in the administration of the National Railway System. I do not know how it is now, but I do know that it was not an uncommon expectation on the part of the public that the department should reinstate employees, purchase ties, and do all manner of things incidental to the administration of the system. That

condition obtained in the past, and I have no doubt it obtains to-day, and what the department is obliged to do is to pass these things on to the board to which each particular instance may relate. Unquestionably representations were made to the Government and, as well, to the Minister of Railways, from day to day with reference to unemployment. There was only one thing for the Government to do, and that was to pass them on to the board whose duty it was to deal with them. And that was done. But so far as the Minister of Railways was concerned, let me make it quite clear that neither he nor any other officer of the Government played any part in deciding what rails it was wise to buy, or what cars it was wise or necessary to rebuild or repair. Not one word was offered by the minister or any officer of the Government as to where cars should be repaired. The Minister of Labour supplied to those who had the deciding of the matter the information with reference tc unemployment in the different centres where rails were manufactured and cars built and where there were industries suitably equipped for carrying on the work. But, as I say, neither the Minister of Railways nor any other officer of the Government had anything to say in the matter.
In response to the request of the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Mitchell), I shall be glad to lay the Order in Council on the Table tomorrow.	.

Listening to the discussion to-night, it appears to me that we are arguing altogether on false premises. If the Canadian National Railway system or public ownership is to be made a success, are we going to continue the policy of making the Canadian National railways the scapegoat in regard to all unemployment throughout the Dominion of Canada? Knowing the Minister of Railways (Mr. Kennedy), as I do, to be a shrewd business man, I do not believe that he will tolerate any such condition as that. If this or any other government is to make a success of the Canadian National railways it is their duty to place these orders where they can be executed at the lowest possible cost; and if there is unemployment to be dealt with in the country, then let the Government have a policy to cope with that situation, in keeping with the efforts that are being made by the local governments and the municipalities in the various provinces. But I contend that it is an entirely wrong principle that, in order to

Supply-Immigration
relieve unemployment in any part of the country, some particular public service, such as the Canadian National railways, should be saddled with a burden which would inevitably be reflected back in the freight rates, in respect of which we have complaints coming from all parts of the country. I think the Government would be well advised if they adhered to strict business principles, and having every confidence in the Minister of Railways, I take it that he will do so..

What is the explanation given by the department as to why their estimates were so far below the requirements?

This vote is required for field and garden seeds to the amount of $7,000. Last spring Indians who had land prepared but were without funds to purchase the necessary seed grain, and having no band funds held in trust by the department, were advanced funds upon the understanding that the cost of the seed would be refunded from the sale of grain raised. On some of the reserves in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta the crops were a failure, and in consequence the Indians are unable to make all the refunds. This vote is required to cover the deficits, as there was no appropriation in the main estimates. Had there been fair crops the whole cost would have been refunded. The Indians who still owe for seed grain will be required to make refunds from next season's crop if they have one, so that eventually the amount of this vote will be refunded, and should be regarded simply as a loan. A statement of the expenditure and refunds is given, if my hon. friend wants it.
As to the supplies for destitute, $34,000, this vote is required to pay for provisions, ammunition and twine delivered under contract during the summer of 1920 by the

Hudson's Bay Company at different points in the Peace river, Athabasca and Mac-kenie river districts. The contractors are required to have their accounts for these supplies certified by the Indian agent to whom delivery of the supplies is made, but through neglect on the part of the Hudson's Bay Company's officer at Edmonton, the certified accounts did not reach the department until after the close of the fiscal year 1920-21, and consequently payment had to be made from the appropriation for the current fiscal year, 1921-22. It became necessary, therefore, to provide for these payments as the appropriation for the fiscal year 1921-22 is insufficient to meet this extra charge. These supplies are delivered annually under contract and are to meet treaty obligations. Hitherto they have always been paid for within the fiscal year in which they are contracted for.
As to the further amount of $3,600 required for general expenses, in the supplementary estimates for 1921-22 the sum of $19,200 was included to pay for 640 acres of land at $30 an acre within the boundaries of Ermineskins reserve in the province of Alberta, but only $12,600 Was appropriated under Vote No. 518. It becomes necessary therefore to ask for a supplementary vote of $3,600 to enable the department to pay the balance due on this land.
The amount asked for is $10,600, not $3,600.

The further amount required for general expenses is $7,000. This with the previous amount will make the $10,600. This vote is required to replace the Indian agent's residence at Fort Smith, Alberta, on the Slave river, accidentally destroyed by fire on February 3 last, and it was absolutely necessary to replace it. Building materials such as hardware, windows, doors, cement, brick, building paper, etc., also a furnace, were purchased at Edmonton and transported to Fort Smith via Peace River, a distance of 988 miles. The necessary lumber was manufactured at the department's sawmill at Fort Smith, but funds had to be provided for wages, etc. The expenditure not being provided for in the main estimates, this vote becomes necessary.

With regard to the minister's explanation of the $3,600, can he tell me whether that is the case of Janse brothers who had a section of land within an Indian reserve that the depart-

Supply-Indians
ment exchanged for a Hudson's Bay section? I remember the negotiations were pending a long while owing to a difference of opinion as to the value of the land.

Under the
terms of the deed of surrender given by the Hudson's Bay Company to the Crown when relinquishing all claim to the lands in Rupert's Land and the Northwest Territories, which entitled the company to claim grants of land up to one-twentieth of all lands set out for settlement within the fertile belt, the section of land referred to passed to the Hudson's Bay Company. In September, 1885, the limits of the Ermineskins Indian reserve were surveyed by this department, in accordance with the terms of the treaty, and this section was included. This reserve was confirmed by Order in Council, dated May 17, 1889.
In 1906 the Hudson's Bay Comil p.m. pany sold this section to Messrs.
Janse brothers, of Calgary, both parties evidently having entered into the transaction in good faith, without the knowledge of its being part of an Indian reserve. Messrs. Janse brothers are unable to make use of their land as it is part of an Indian reserve. The department has endeavoured to arrange the matter by obtaining an exchange of lands, but the Indians refused to give a surrender, and the only recourse is to purchase from Messrs. Janse brothers. They have signified their willingness to accept $30 per acre, and to assign to the Crown whatever title they have received from the Hudson's Bay Company.
The price paid seems to me rather high. When was the arrangement completed for the purchase of it?
Some months ago, I am informed-before December 6.

That may be. I remember when I was in the department we tried for years to make the exchange and we had great difficulty in doing it. We sought to refer it to an arbitration, but never were able to get that done. The price was below $30 an acre. But I do not just see why this should be in last year's estimates; it would be provided for in next year's estimates in the ordinary way.

Some appropriation was made in the estimates of last
year to cover this, but evidently it was not sufficient.

The estimated expenditure for this service for the fiscal year 1921-22 was $31,000, but owing to circumstances over which the department has no control, it proved inadequate to meet all the demands due to various causes, namely, failure of crops in some districts, fishing restrictions imposed upon the Indians by the federal authorities, unemployment and sickness amongst the Indian population of about 25,000. Each agency was apportioned its share, and instructions were issued that these amounts were not to be exceeded without first obtaining the authority of the department. There are sixteen agencies in the province and extra grants had to be made to several upon representations made by the agents that unless the amounts first allowed were not increased, there would be suffering amongst the Indians through no fault of their own. On humanitarian grounds, therefore, the department was bound to come to their relief and authorize increased expenditure.

Relief in the form of food, clothing, ammunition, twine, medicines and medical attendance, is provided for Indians and Eskimo who live in the more remote districts of the Dominion and are dependent entirely on the hunt for their existence.

This relief is administered by the fur trading companies at their various posts [DOT]where t'he department has, no resident agents, and the department has endeavoured from time to time to control and curtail this expenditure as much as possible by instructing these companies that supplies should only be issued to relieve distress amongst Indians and Eskimo who are too old or unable through sickness, etc., to hunt their own living; and at times to others who are in distress through failure of the hunt.
The department is compelled to adopt this method of affording rdlief to these natives when in distress, but every possible care is taken in checking the accounts through missionaries or members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Polite, where available, besides which they are very carefully scrutinized in the department before payment is made, with a view to preventing abuses which might arise from the companies outfitting Indians who are capable hunters and who should not be a charge on the government. There are, therefore, inherent difficulties of management which the department has had to overcome, with a certain degree of success, but until these remote districts are more closely connected with civilization, and until the department is represented by local officers, the conditions will not he entirely satisfactory.
Owing to the remote situation of the posts, where relief is issued, the cost is naturally high, consequent upon the excessive cost of transportation.

Item agreed to.
Indian Education-further amount required, $35,615.45.

I only have one criticism to offer as to this item, and in doing that I can only take the same ground that was taken by hon. members to my right in the case of estimates of another department. When the Main Estimates containing the vote for Indian education was brought down a decrease of something over $101,000 was observable. Some of us took exception to that on the ground that education was one thing that should not be neglected. In the course of the discussion that followed we were assured that provision would be made in the Supplementary Estimates. Provision has been made for a certain amount but I still notice a decrease compared with last year of a little over $66,000.
These estimates relate to last year. There are still further supplementary estimates to be presented.

Item agreed to.
Board of Commerce-further amount required to provide for arrears of salary of the secretary from July 1, 1921, to March 31, 1922, $3,000.
This ends the Board of Commerce.
This winds it up?
Yes, it covers the funeral expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Financially and otherwise.

Item agreed to.
Expenses of the Canadian Delegates to the Economic and Financial Conference at Genoa (Governor General's warrant, February 20, 1922), $25,000.

Might I ask the Prime Minister the circumstances under which the Canadian Government were asked to participate in the Genoa Conference? Did we receive an invitation direct from Italy, as I understand the other countries that are sending delegates to this conference did?
An invitation direct from the Italian government to the Government of Canada asking us to send delegates was received.
When did the conference commence?
My recollection is that it was about three weeks ago.
Why is this charged against last year's expenditure?

I may inform my right hon. friend that it was necessary for the delegates to leave Canada during the last fiscal year to reach Genoa in time, and that the whole amount has not been used up. I am informed that there is an unexpended balance of $8,852.62 which has lapsed and must be revoted when we come to the estimates for this year.
When did the delegates leave Canada?
I have not the exact date here, but it was some time in the last fiscal year.

Some time in March, because the conference opened on April 5.

Supply-Genoa Conference

Even if they did leave Canada toward the end of the fiscal year that would not make it a legitimate charge against last year's expenditure. It would be a very small amount that could possibly be justified, if anything at all, against last year's expenditures. It should have been included in this year's expenditures in the usual way.
An estimate was put in about the middle of March.
But even so the conference is being held this year.
Shall the resolution carry?

I object to this resolution carrying. I, think the Government should be fair in this matter. It is not a very large item, but it shows a rather too ardent desire to shove this year's expenditures into last year.
Oh, oh.
Hon. members think it is a joke. Well, there is something of a joke about it.
Not at all. It is impossible to make provision for any delegates attending the conference except by Governor General's warrant.

Very well if there was a little money required to carry them on their way the Governor General's warrant might have covered it. The whole thing might have been covered by one warant but to charge it to last year's expenditure is not right.
The delegates were each given an advance of $8,000, 1 think. That does not seem a very large amount to take over for such a purpose.

Particularly for Sir
Charles Gordon.

The hon. member
thinks he is a pretty expensive man.

I am sure he needed
money before he started.

The proper way for the Government to have acted was to have advanced such money as was essential if the delegates had to leave in March, and to advance the balance the coming year. Then the thing could have been done quite rightly without charging the entire amount to last year. That seems to be the general policy adopted-to make last year pay for this year's work.
I may point out that the invitation was received on January 21 and it was at that time the Government began to make this arrangement.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister if he can give us any information as to the nature of the instructions given to these delegates as far as their work at Genoa is concerned?

Generally
they were asked to participate in the conference, and to keep the Government informed as to any matters which it was thought advisable to bring to the Government's attention. I think my hon. friend had placed before him the proceedings at the Cannes Conference which outlined the work to be done at the Genoa Conference, and the duties of the delegates would pertain to the programme outlined there. The delegates were instructed to observe those matters pertaining more essentially to the European countries, but to pay particular attention to those matters relating to the Dominion and not to take final action with respect to the signing of any treaties or agreements without fully informing the Government of the nature of the proposed treaties before final action was determined upon.

And receiving the
Government's approval.

Yes, and
also to see that all agreements or treaties that were signed were made subject to the approval of Parliament.

I see by the press that the conference has determined the question of the mandate of Great Britain over Palestine. Can the Prime Minister tell us if any instructions have been given our delegates with regard to their action in the matter?

No, they
have an absolutely free hand in regard to Palestine.
Can the minister tell us what has been accomplished by S'.r Charles Gordon and his co-representative on behalf of Canada in the way of economic regeneration?

The Government has asked Sir Charles Gordon to give a report at the end of the proceedings, and I will have pleasure in seeing that that report is brought down in due course.

Supply-Criminal Code
As yet they have not any information as to anything being accomplished.

I do not think the world has word of anything being accomplished in the conference, our delegates are in the same position as delegates of other countries, and I presume they are doing just as well as the others.
I observe that certain countries are in danger of losing their representatives on account of the high cost of living at Genoa. Has the Government considered that matter?
Yes, I think their expenses are being paid by the Italian government, so that, as far as this Government is concerned, we have escaped.

Item agreed to.
Reprinting Criminal Code including 1920-21 amendment, $1,500.
Reprinting annual statutes, years 1907, 1908, 1909, 1910, 1912, 1913, 1914, 1915, 1919, 1920, $9,100.

I think this is charged under the wrong heading. It is charged to legislation. The reprinting of the Criminal Code is part of the administration of justice and I think should be charged to that department, and probably "reprinting annual statutes'' should also come under that department. I do not know whether any one desires the change to be made at the present time, but I think for the future notice should be taken of it, and it should be put in its proper vote in the Department of Justice, and not under legislation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman is quite right in regard to that, although this work has been done by the Law Department of the House of Commons.

I did see
some explanation to the effect that this was to cover the cost of material at the Printing Bureau, and that copies of these statutes were for sale on application.
Why is it in last year's estimates?
I should think probably the 1921 amendments would be done pretty well in the early part of the year.

I do not know whether I am in order in asking the Government whether it is their intention to revise the
Criminal Code. This code was introduced about 30 years ago and no revision has taken place since. It is customary to revise the ordinary statutes every ten years. I know that the matter was discussed at a recent meeting of the Council of the Canadian Bar Association, and it was thought advisable to urge upon the Government the necessity of a revision of this code, because many amendments have been introduced in the past 30 years.
It was revised in 1906, when all the statutes were revised.
That is 16 years ago, and I think something should be done in the matter of consolidating it and bringing it into some kind of shape.

I might say, for the information of the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs), that he can obtain a copy of the Criminal Code which is completely revised, with the exception of the amendments passed last year. The revision has 'been made from time to time by the Parliamentary Counsel, and the code in its completed and amended form can be obtained from the King's Printer.

I do not mean the ordinary revision, but I refer to the question of overhauling the entire code and bringing it abreast of the times. There are very many matters which I think ought to be re-codified and re-discussed, if I may use that expression. The Criminal Code must naturally keep abreast of public opinion, and, as it is the rule in other countries to have their criminal legislation gone over from time to time, I think it would be well that we should deal with that now. There are many things in the Criminal Code that might be changed, as many things have happened during the past sixteen years. The Criminal Code is an important piece of legislation, and it should be given more attention than it has been receiving during the past sixteen years.

What my hon. friend has said has application to the Criminal Code, but the time has long since passed when the whole of the statutes of Canada should have been revised. There has been no revision of the statutes since 1906, when the Criminal Code was revised, consolidated and passed. The work of revision of the statutes which, I think, should take place every ten years, is long overdue, but I understand the work was well under way last autumn. Very substantial progress had been made on that work on, I believe, very
Supply-Agriculture

satisfactory financial conditions and terms. It would not take very long now to complete the work, and I sincerely hope the Government will prosecute it to a successful conclusion at the earliest posible moment.
To what extent was the work done last autumn?
I should think three-quarters of the work had been done.
By whom?

Mr. O'Connor had done a good deal of it. I do not remember just what the arrangements were; but they provided for complete revision at a cost very substantially less than it had been done before, although ordinarily the cost would be very much greater now. I think the Government would do well to review the whole matter thoroughly, because I thought it an excellent arrangement for revision.

In matters of that kind, is it not necessary to have reports made from time to time to the Government as to the advisability of changes, additions, amendments and so on in legislation? I do not mean in the matter of consolidating the statutes, but in overhauling an entire statute.
That, of course, is another matter which hardly should be committed to the man in charge of revision.
To Parliament?

Yes. It is certainly
time we had a complete revision; the arrangement made for revision was economical, and the work was going on most expertly. I hope the Government will continue the revision and have it completed.
How long was Mr. O'Connor employed on this work?
I could not say; but Mr. O'Connor is a man, who, when he is on a task, works night and day. He is a prodigious worker when he is at work, and he is a very efficient man in that class of work.
What salary was paid to him for the work?
I could not say what was paid. I knew at one time what the arrangement was, and it can easily be ascertained.

I hardly think there was any such

understanding about the matter as that given by my right hon. friend. The leader of the Opposition says that there was an arrangement with Mr. O'Connor about this work. We all know that Mr. O'Connor is a very capable man and a very efficient worker in anything which he undertakes. But it must not be supposed that it rests with this Government to continue the arrangement, because the arrangement was cut off by the late government many months before they went out of office, and they paid Mr. O'Connor for the work he did.
I do not think that is right.
If there is anything to be done henceforth, what will be done must be taken up afresh and some new arrangement made.
I really think my hon. friend is wrong because I knew nothing about that.
My right hon. friend will find that I am not wrong.
By what officer was this done?
The matter, as regards the settling up, was done by the Deputy Minister of Justice.

I do not know what the Deputy Minister of Justice may have felt or thought or done about the matter; but I do not think the government, as a government, authorized the cancellation of any arrangement. If so, I knew nothing of it, and I would be surprised that such is the fact.
My right hon. friend may rest assured that I have the correct information, because I have it from Mr. O'Connor himself. It is not second hand at all.
I talked to him not long ago, and I did not get that impression at all.
Item agreed to.
Agriculture-for stock grazing and feeding- Governor General's warrants, December 1, 1921, and February 7, 1922, $50,000.
Will the minister kindly give us some explanation of this item?

speechtext:
This heading is somewhat misleading. I do not know exactly why it

Redistribution
